entries.name: Literary Historical Fiction
entries.description: The reconstructed past as a claim on truth, not backdrop; the risk is detail burying the mind.
entries.principle: The literary historical novel treats the reconstructed past as a claim on the truth rather than a backdrop, asking the research to serve interiority instead of smothering it; the distinctive risk is that accumulated detail buries the consciousness the book exists to render, so that period becomes a display of furniture rather than a lens on a mind.
entries.example: Penelope Fitzgerald's The Blue Flower (1995) reconstructs the young Novalis in late-eighteenth-century Saxony almost entirely through implication, carrying its research so lightly that the world arrives as sensibility rather than exposition.
entries.application: Draft the consciousness first and let the verified detail enter only where a character would actually notice it; if a researched fact does not change what someone thinks or feels, it is scenery and can be cut.

entries.name: The Family and Dynastic Saga
entries.description: A bloodline made protagonist; the past read across generations, where causality can go slack.
entries.principle: The saga makes a bloodline or a house the true protagonist and stakes its claim about the past on continuity, arguing that the meaning of a period is only visible across the generations it shapes; the craft danger is that causality goes slack once no single life spans the arc.
entries.example: Sigrid Undset's Kristin Lavransdatter (1920 to 1922) follows one fourteenth-century Norwegian woman from childhood to death so that the medieval order is felt as the weight of a whole life rather than argued.
entries.application: Give every generation a decision that constrains the next, so the passage of time reads as consequence rather than mere chronology, and resist the temptation to let a later character simply inherit an earlier one's conflict unchanged.

entries.name: The Biographical Novel
entries.description: A documented real life fictionalised; the craft problem is where archive ends and interpolation begins.
entries.principle: The biographical novel fictionalises a documented real life, and its claim about the past is answerable in a way invented-character fiction is not, because a reader can check it; the governing craft problem is where the archive stops and the novelist must interpolate, and whether that seam is honestly signalled.
entries.example: Marguerite Yourcenar's Memoirs of Hadrian (1951) stages a Roman emperor's reconstruction as a dying man's letter, making the gaps in the record into gaps the narrator himself must reach across.
entries.application: Mark for yourself every point where you have invented past the documented life, decide what kind of claim each invention makes, and let the author's note or the texture of the prose tell the reader which is which.

entries.name: Pure Period Reconstruction
entries.description: Total immersion in which the world itself is the argument; the failure mode is inertia.
entries.principle: In total-immersion reconstruction the world itself is the argument, and the claim about the past is that a vanished mentality can be inhabited whole; the failure mode is inertia, the catalogue of accurate things standing in for a story.
entries.example: Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose (1980) reconstructs a fourteenth-century monastery so completely that its theology, its library and its politics generate the plot rather than decorate it.
entries.application: Test every immersive passage against a plot function; if a magnificently researched scene could be removed without changing what happens or what a character understands, the reconstruction has become an end in itself.

entries.name: The Multi-Generational National Epic
entries.description: A people's history through a spanning narrative; keep private lives legible against the scale.
entries.principle: The national epic reconstructs a people's history through a spanning narrative and claims to explain how a country became itself; the pressure is to keep private lives legible against the scale, so that history is dramatised rather than narrated.
entries.example: Yaa Gyasi's Homegoing (2016) traces two branches of a family from eighteenth-century Ghana to the present, letting each self-contained chapter carry a stage of the transatlantic history the whole book indicts.
entries.application: Anchor each movement of the sweep in one person's irreversible choice, and let the largest historical forces reach the reader only through what they cost a named individual.

entries.name: The Swashbuckler and Adventure Historical
entries.description: The period as a playground for pace and set-piece; frankly popular rather than documentary.
entries.principle: The adventure historical treats the period as a playground for pace and set-piece, and its claim about the past is frankly popular rather than documentary; it is a large share of what readers buy, and a reference work that patronises it is both snobbish and inaccurate.
entries.example: Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers (1844) subordinates seventeenth-century fact to momentum and honour, and earns its liberties by never pretending to the reconstruction it declines.
entries.application: Decide openly that you are writing for velocity, then keep the period's hard constraints (distance, weaponry, communication) honest even while you play with the soft ones, because an adventure collapses the moment its physical world cheats.

entries.name: The Nautical and Age-of-Sail Novel
entries.description: A ship made a complete society, its authenticity resting on exact yet nearly invisible rigour.
entries.principle: The sailing-navy novel makes a ship into a complete society and stakes its authenticity on technical rigour that must be exact and yet nearly invisible; the claim about the past is that a lost working world can be reconstructed from its own vocabulary.
entries.example: Patrick O'Brian's Master and Commander (1969) renders the Royal Navy of the Napoleonic wars through seamanship so precise it functions as characterisation, then trusts the reader to sail on partial understanding.
entries.application: Learn the working detail thoroughly, then deliver only the fraction a competent crew member would remark on, so the expertise reads as lived competence rather than a manual.

entries.name: The Frontier and Revisionist Historical
entries.description: A settlement myth increasingly told to correct it, romance held against documented violence.
entries.principle: The frontier novel reconstructs a settlement myth and increasingly claims to correct it, setting the romance of conquest against its documented violence; the craft pressure is to hold both the myth's pull and its falsity in the same book.
entries.example: Larry McMurtry's Lonesome Dove (1985) honours the cattle-drive epic while systematically recording its tedium, cruelty and waste, so the elegy and the correction arrive together.
entries.application: Identify the received myth your setting carries, then decide scene by scene whether you are indulging it or dismantling it, and never let the reader mistake which without a reason.

entries.name: Historical Fiction from Oral Tradition
entries.description: The record is itself communal narrative; treating oral tradition as a mere gap is the error.
entries.principle: Here the record is itself narrative, communal and mythic rather than archival, and the claim about the past runs through testimony and inherited memory; oral tradition is not an absence in the record but a different record, with its own custodianship and failure modes, and treating it as a gap is the error.
entries.example: Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987) builds its history of slavery from what testimony and haunting carry rather than from the ledger, insisting that the unwritten past is fully real and differently held.
entries.application: When the written archive is silent about a community, do not conclude the record is empty; ask who holds it, in what form, and whether it is yours to take, and let that answer shape what you are permitted to invent.

entries.name: The Classical and Antiquity Novel
entries.description: An alien mentality entered without modernising it; the failure is present-day feeling in period dress.
entries.principle: The antiquity novel reconstructs a mentality genuinely alien to modern readers and claims it can be entered without being modernised; the failure mode is a present-day sensibility in period dress, feeling the ancient world would not have felt.
entries.example: Robert Graves's I, Claudius (1934) narrates imperial Rome from inside its assumptions about family, power and the gods, so the horror reads as the narrator's normality rather than the author's judgement.
entries.application: Establish what your period took for granted that a modern reader would find monstrous, then let characters hold those assumptions without flinching, reserving any modern verdict for the structure rather than the dialogue.

entries.name: The Medieval Novel
entries.description: A theocentric world where faith is the air, rendered without mockery or sentiment.
entries.principle: The medieval novel reconstructs a theocentric world in which faith is not a theme but the air, and claims a modern reader can be made to feel belief as lived reality; the pressure is to render a total worldview without either mocking it or sentimentalising it.
entries.example: Ken Follett's The Pillars of the Earth (1989) grounds a twelfth-century cathedral's construction in the economics and devotion of the age, making the medieval understanding of work, God and hierarchy structurally load-bearing.
entries.application: Treat the period's cosmology as fact within the book, so that miracles, damnation and the just price operate as real forces on decisions, not as colour a secular narrator observes from outside.

entries.name: The Tudor and Early-Modern Novel
entries.description: Terrain so saturated the craft problem is defamiliarisation: making the known story strange again.
entries.principle: The Tudor novel works terrain so saturated that its central craft problem is defamiliarisation, and its claim about the past is that a story everyone thinks they know can be made strange and contingent again.
entries.example: Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall (2009) re-sees the Henrician court through Thomas Cromwell rather than the doomed queens, and the shift of vantage makes an exhausted period urgent and uncertain.
entries.application: Find the vantage the standard version omits, and narrate the famous outcome as if it were still in doubt, denying the reader the comfort of the ending they already carry.

entries.name: The Napoleonic and Revolutionary-War Novel
entries.description: An age as both military machine and Romantic idea; keep its materiality legible under the glamour.
entries.principle: The Napoleonic novel treats an age as simultaneously a military machine and a Romantic idea, and claims to reconstruct both the logistics and the myth; the pressure is to keep the campaign's brutal materiality legible under the era's glamour.
entries.example: Bernard Cornwell's Sharpe's Eagle (1981) delivers the Peninsular War through a ranker's-eye view where powder, supply and rank decide outcomes the Romantic version obscures.
entries.application: Let the period's material constraints (marching distances, black-powder misfires, the pace of orders) drive your battles, so the Romantic surface sits on a machine the reader can feel grinding underneath.

entries.name: The Age of Revolutions and Enlightenment Novel
entries.description: Ideas in motion, mob against individual; the danger is characters who lecture rather than choose.
entries.principle: This subgenre dramatises ideas in motion and the collision of the mob with the individual, claiming that a period's arguments can be made to live as action; the danger is characters who lecture rather than choose.
entries.example: Hilary Mantel's A Place of Greater Safety (1992) follows Danton, Robespierre and Desmoulins through the French Revolution so that revolutionary theory is always someone's fatal, specific decision.
entries.application: Convert every idea the period is arguing about into a choice with a body count, and let no character state a principle they are not about to be tested on.

entries.name: The Neo-Victorian Novel
entries.description: The nineteenth century reconstructed with modern awareness; the trap is knowingness over feeling.
entries.principle: The neo-Victorian novel reconstructs the nineteenth century with deliberate modern awareness, and its claim about the past is doubled, being also a claim about how we now read that past; the trap is knowingness, cleverness about the period substituting for feeling within it.
entries.example: A. S. Byatt's Possession (1990) braids a Victorian love story with the present-day scholars pursuing it, using the anachronistic frame as subject rather than as an accident to be hidden.
entries.application: Decide whether your modern perspective is a tool or a tic; if the narration keeps winking at how much more the reader knows than the characters, cut the wink and let the period's own terms carry the scene.

entries.name: The Great War Novel
entries.description: Industrialised trauma represented without aestheticising it or retreating into numbers.
entries.principle: The First World War novel confronts industrialised trauma and claims that a rupture which broke the era's own language can nonetheless be represented; the pressure is to render mechanised horror without either aestheticising it or retreating into numbers.
entries.example: Pat Barker's Regeneration (1991) approaches the trenches through a military hospital, so that the war's damage is legible in the treatment of shell shock rather than in the spectacle of battle.
entries.application: Find the oblique vantage (the hospital, the letter home, the returned survivor) that lets you show the wound without staging the atrocity as entertainment, and let period silence do work that description cannot.

entries.name: The Second World War, Occupation and Holocaust Novel
entries.description: Proximity to living survivors and atrocity; the failure is catastrophe as backdrop for uplift.
entries.principle: This subgenre carries the library's heaviest proximity to living survivors and to atrocity, and its claim about the past is inseparable from the ethics of imagining it; the failure is to use catastrophe as a backdrop for uplift.
entries.example: Irène Némirovsky's Suite Française illuminates the problem from its own edge, written under the Occupation in 1940 to 1942 and published only in 2004, a book set in its author's present that time turned into history.
entries.application: Before using an atrocity as material, decide what kind of claim you are making about people whose descendants are alive, and let the book answer for it rather than borrow its gravity.

entries.name: Slavery and Its Aftermath
entries.description: The enslaved rendered as subjects, not setting; the question is whose voice and whose archive.
entries.principle: This subgenre reconstructs slavery and its long consequences and stakes everything on representing the enslaved as subjects rather than as the setting for someone else's drama; the central question is whose voice and whose archive, when the record was kept by the enslavers.
entries.example: Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad (2016) literalises the escape network as a working railway, using a controlled anachronism to make a claim about the record's silences that a documentary approach could not.
entries.application: Locate whose interiority your book centres, and if the enslaved are present only as suffering observed by others, the reconstruction has reproduced the archive's own erasure; build the point of view from the silenced side.

entries.name: The Colonial and Postcolonial Historical
entries.description: Writing back to empire and contesting its record without adopting the frame the sources impose.
entries.principle: This subgenre writes back to empire and contests the colonizer's record, claiming the authority to narrate a history the archive framed from one side; the craft pressure is to reconstruct a pre-colonial or colonised world without adopting the frame the sources impose.
entries.example: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) rebuilds an Igbo society at the moment of colonial contact from inside its own logic, answering the European account by refusing its vantage.
entries.application: Interrogate the provenance of every source you rely on, ask what interest it served, and where the only records are the colonizer's, write toward what they were structured to omit rather than paraphrasing what they chose to keep.

entries.name: The Immigrant and Diaspora Historical
entries.description: An old country recovered through memory and inheritance; the past doubly mediated by displacement.
entries.principle: The diaspora historical reconstructs an old country from the distance of exile and claims that a homeland can be recovered through memory and inheritance rather than residence; the pressure is that the past is doubly mediated, by history and by displacement.
entries.example: Amitav Ghosh's Sea of Poppies (2008) assembles a nineteenth-century world of indenture and opium across the Indian Ocean, reconstructing a dispersal from the vantage of its scattered descendants.
entries.application: Make the distance itself part of the subject, so that what has been lost or garbled in transmission becomes material rather than error, and the homeland arrives as something reconstructed rather than remembered.

entries.name: The Nueva Novela Histórica
entries.description: Distrust of the official record through metafiction and anachronism; the risk is mannerism.
entries.principle: The Latin American new historical novel distrusts the official record as method, using metafiction and deliberate anachronism to claim that the past is contested terrain rather than settled fact; the risk is that the technique becomes a mannerism detached from the history it interrogates.
entries.example: Alejo Carpentier's The Kingdom of This World (1949) reconstructs the Haitian Revolution through a frankly marvellous lens, arguing that the region's history cannot be told in the realist grammar of the archive that suppressed it.
entries.application: Let any anachronism or metafictional move be an argument about how this particular history was recorded and by whom, not a stylistic flourish; if the device is not saying something about the record, it is decoration.

entries.name: The Secret History
entries.description: A hidden causal layer behind real events, invented into the gaps without breaking a known fact.
entries.principle: The secret history posits a hidden causal layer behind documented events and claims to reveal what really drove them, on the strict condition that it never contradicts the known record; the pressure is to invent into the gaps without breaking a single verifiable fact.
entries.example: Iain Pears's An Instance of the Fingerpost (1997) sets four unreliable narrators against one another in Restoration Oxford, building a concealed truth that slots precisely into the documented history without dislodging it.
entries.application: Map the fixed points of the real record first, then invent only in the spaces between them, so that your hidden explanation could in principle be true rather than requiring the reader to forget what happened.

entries.name: Biofiction of the Recovered Voice
entries.description: First-person narrative for the archive's silenced; recovering a voice or ventriloquising one.
entries.principle: This subgenre gives first-person narrative to real people the archive silenced, and its claim about the past is an act of restitution; the pressure is that speaking for the erased can either recover a voice or ventriloquise one, and the line between them is the whole ethical problem.
entries.example: Maryse Condé's I, Tituba, Black Witch of Salem (1986) narrates the Salem trials through their most documented yet least heard figure, reconstructing an interior life from the few lines the record allowed her.
entries.application: Ask whether your reconstruction restores agency the record removed or merely projects a modern voice onto a convenient silence, and let the answer govern how far you claim to know what the person thought.

entries.name: Historical Romance (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to romance-reference; the historical pressure is the ending the period would not have granted.
entries.principle: This card hands off to romance-reference, which owns the courtship structure and the guarantee that the promise is paid; the specifically historical pressure is different. Romance asks whether the promise is paid; Historical asks whether the ending the period would not have granted has been engineered into these characters' specific circumstances rather than into the society.
entries.example: Diana Gabaldon's Outlander (1991) earns its across-the-centuries union through individual contrivance, and the historical question is whether the escape is built into the two people's situation rather than falsely into the age.
entries.application: When a period would have denied your couple their ending, locate the plausibility in their specific circumstances (rank, isolation, exception) rather than quietly liberalising the whole society to permit it.

entries.name: Historical Crime (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to mystery-crime-thriller; the pressure is whether the period had the investigative apparatus assumed.
entries.principle: This card hands off to mystery-crime-thriller-reference, which owns the fairness of the investigation; the specifically historical pressure is different. MCT asks whether the investigation is fair; Historical asks whether the period had the investigative apparatus the plot assumes, and what policing meant before it existed.
entries.example: Ellis Peters's A Morbid Taste for Bones (1977) sets its detection in a twelfth century with no forensics and no police, so the inquiry must run on testimony, standing and canon law. The award named for Ellis Peters postdates her, a trap to note.
entries.application: Audit your detective's methods against what the period actually permitted; if the solution depends on an epistemology (fingerprints, autopsy, a police force) that did not yet exist, the crime is being solved by anachronism.

entries.name: Historical Horror (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to horror-reference; the pressure is atrocity used as material whose descendants are alive.
entries.principle: This card hands off to horror-reference, which owns the question of what the fear is of; the specifically historical pressure is different. Horror asks what the fear is of; Historical asks whether the atrocity being used as horror material happened to people whose descendants are alive.
entries.example: Dan Simmons's The Terror (2007) grafts a supernatural predator onto the historically documented loss of the Franklin expedition, and the historical question is what is owed to the real dead the frame conscripts.
entries.application: Before turning a documented horror into genre machinery, decide whether the suffering you are mining belongs to a living community, and let that determine whether the supernatural illuminates the history or merely exploits it.

entries.name: Historical War and Military (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to the war pack; the historical pressure is who may narrate a war, and from whose archive.
entries.principle: This card hands off to the planned war-and-military pack, which will own combat and command; the specifically historical pressure is different. The war pack will ask about combat and command; Historical asks who is permitted to narrate a war, and what a battle looks like from the losing archive.
entries.example: Michael Shaara's The Killer Angels (1974) narrates Gettysburg from both commands, raising the historical question of whose account survives to be dramatised and whose was written by the winners.
entries.application: Choose your narrating vantage deliberately, and test whether the battle you are reconstructing looks the same from the side whose records did not survive; if you can only see it from the victor's, say so.

entries.name: Alternate History (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to sf-reference; the historical pressure is what the counterfactual is actually for.
entries.principle: This card hands off to sf-reference, which owns the rigour of the counterfactual; the specifically historical pressure is different. SF asks whether the counterfactual is rigorous; Historical asks what the counterfactual is for, which real outcome it is arguing about.
entries.example: Robert Harris's Fatherland (1992) reconstructs a Europe in which the Reich survived, and the historical charge of the book is the actual genocide the counterfactual is arguing about, not the mechanism of divergence.
entries.application: Before engineering a point of divergence, decide what real historical claim the counterfactual is making; if the alternate world is not arguing about something that genuinely happened, it is a puzzle rather than a history.

entries.name: The Documentary and Nonfiction Novel
entries.description: Real names bound to acknowledged invention; the seams between answerable and made must be declared.
entries.principle: The nonfiction novel binds real names and real events to acknowledged invention, and its claim about the past is a hybrid that must declare its own seams; the pressure is that the reader's trust depends on knowing which parts are answerable to the record.
entries.example: Thomas Keneally's Schindler's Ark (1982) reconstructs a documented rescue through novelistic technique while signalling its factual spine, sitting deliberately on the border between history and fiction.
entries.application: Make the contract explicit somewhere in the book, so the reader knows the events are real and the interior lives are reconstructed, and never let a novelistic invention masquerade as a documented fact.

entries.name: The National-Founding Romance
entries.description: Scott's form: a nation's past as formative narrative, with propaganda as its besetting hazard.
entries.principle: This is the form Walter Scott invented, reconstructing a nation's past as narrative and often in service of building or mythologising it; the claim about the past is openly formative, which is also its hazard, since nation-building fiction shades easily into propaganda.
entries.example: Walter Scott's Waverley (1814) set its story sixty years before its writing and taught the culture to imagine its own history as a novel, founding the genre and its patriotic uses at once.
entries.application: Where your book is helping a nation narrate itself, watch the seam between reconstruction and myth-making, and decide consciously whether you are examining the founding story or merely retelling it in its own flattering terms.

entries.name: The Archive Is an Artefact of Power
entries.description: The archive is what powerful institutions chose to keep, not a random sample of the past.
entries.principle: What survives from the past is not a random sample of it; it is what institutions with the means to keep records chose to keep, about the matters those institutions cared about. Treating the archive as a neutral deposit inherits its biases unexamined and mistakes the powerful's account for the past itself.
entries.example: Michel-Rolph Trouillot's Silencing the Past (1995) argues that the historical record is produced by power at every stage, so that a document's presence records an interest served, not a fact neutrally preserved.
entries.application: Before trusting any body of sources, ask whose interests built and kept it, then treat what it contains as evidence about those interests as much as about the events it appears to report.

entries.name: The State Records What It Taxes, Prosecutes and Owns
entries.description: The state records what it taxes, prosecutes and owns; the poor appear only where they cross it.
entries.principle: A state generates documents about taxation, litigation, crime, property and conscription, so people enter its record mainly where they cross a state interest. The propertyless and the illiterate appear as defendants, paupers on a relief roll, or names in a muster, and are otherwise under-documented by design, not by accident.
entries.example: England's Domesday Book (1086) records landholding and taxable value in exhaustive detail while saying nothing of the inner life of the villein it counts as an asset.
entries.application: Ask what your period's record-making apparatus was built to see; a character invisible to that apparatus must be reconstructed from the margins of documents made for other purposes, not from a record that was never kept.

entries.name: The Survival Lottery
entries.description: The survival lottery: fire, war and damp leave an unrepresentative remnant of the past.
entries.principle: Which sources reach us is shaped by fire, war, damp, deliberate loss and the physics of materials, and the survivors are not representative. Durable media over-represent themselves, and a catastrophe can erase a paper archive while fixing a clay one.
entries.example: The 1922 destruction of the Public Record Office of Ireland in the Four Courts fire wiped out roughly seven centuries of records, while in ancient Mesopotamia the fires that destroyed palaces baked and preserved the cuneiform tablet archives, as at Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh.
entries.application: Treat a gap in the surviving record as a fact about survival, not about the past, and decide whether what your book needs was likely never written, written and lost, or written and held somewhere you have not looked.

entries.name: An Absence Can Be the Trace of an Act
entries.description: An absence can be the trace of an act; erasure is a historical event with agents and motives.
entries.principle: Records are sometimes destroyed to erase a person or a claim, so a silence in the archive can itself be evidence that someone acted to produce it. The erasure is a historical event with agents and motives.
entries.example: Roman damnatio memoriae chiselled condemned names from inscriptions, as with Geta after Caracalla in 211, leaving a defacement that documents the very act of erasure it was meant to complete.
entries.application: When the record goes conspicuously quiet around a powerful person's enemy or a regime's predecessor, consider dramatising the erasure itself, and do not mistake an engineered silence for the absence of a story.

entries.name: Locate Which Moment the Silence Entered
entries.description: Locate which of four stages the silence entered, to know if the gap is fillable or unrecoverable.
entries.principle: Silence can be introduced at four distinct stages: the making of sources, the making of archives, the making of narratives, and the assignment of retrospective significance. Knowing which stage silenced your subject tells you whether the gap is fillable, held elsewhere, or structurally unrecoverable.
entries.example: Michel-Rolph Trouillot's Silencing the Past (1995) sets out these four moments as a working analysis, showing that a person can be written out at the source, at the archive, at the narrative, or only later when history decides what mattered.
entries.application: For any gap your book must cross, identify at which of the four moments it was created; a subject never recorded at all is a different craft problem from one recorded and then filtered out of every subsequent history.

entries.name: Unthinkable History
entries.description: Unthinkable history: an interpretive frame, not a shredder, can do the erasing.
entries.principle: An event can be silenced not by the suppression of documents but by an interpretive frame that cannot register it, so that contemporaries who had the facts still could not see what was happening. The frame, not the shredder, does the erasing.
entries.example: Trouillot argues the Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804, the only successful large-scale slave revolt to found a state, was literally unthinkable within the categories of its Western contemporaries, and so was written down and simultaneously not understood.
entries.application: Ask what your period could not conceive, and where a real event exceeded its own era's frame, dramatise the gap between what people recorded and what they were unable to comprehend they were recording.

entries.name: The Monument That Effaces the Man
entries.description: Retrospective significance: a later monument or narrative can efface the person beneath it.
entries.principle: Retrospective significance reassigns meaning, so that a later narrative or a surviving structure can overwrite the person it was built upon. What endures may be the effacement rather than the record.
entries.example: Trouillot's account of the Sans Souci palace, built by Henri Christophe, set against Colonel Jean-Baptiste Sans Souci whom Christophe had killed, shows a monument absorbing and erasing the man whose name it now carries.
entries.application: When a place, a title or a legend has swallowed the person beneath it, consider recovering the buried figure as your subject, and treat the famous surface as the act of forgetting to be undone.

entries.name: Holding the Archive Is Holding the Authority to Read It
entries.description: Holding the archive is holding the authority to read it; being in it is not the same as being true.
entries.principle: The archive is founded by an act of power: the place where documents were kept was also where their meaning was authorised. Whoever controls the archive controls the claim about what it says, which is why being in the archive is not the same as being true.
entries.example: Jacques Derrida's Archive Fever (French 1995, English 1996) locates authority in the arkhe, the magistrate's house where records were both stored and interpreted, making custody and interpretation inseparable.
entries.application: Ask who held and curated the sources your book relies on, and treat their arrangement and emphasis as an argument that was made, not a neutral order you can simply adopt.

entries.name: The Colonial Archive Was Built to Govern, Not to Remember
entries.description: The colonial archive was built to govern, so its categories encode the colonizer's project.
entries.principle: Colonial records were instruments of rule, made to count, classify and control the governed, so their categories encode the colonizer's project. Reading them as neutral description reproduces that project in the guise of fact.
entries.example: Bernard Cohn's work on colonial knowledge in British India, commonly cited as Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge, traces how the census, the survey and the codification of law manufactured the very categories they claimed only to record.
entries.application: Where your only sources on a colonised people are the colonizer's census, cadastre and criminal ethnography, write toward what those instruments were structured to miss rather than paraphrasing the order they imposed.

entries.name: The Gendered Archive
entries.description: The gendered archive files the married woman under a man; she surfaces as widow, defendant or witness.
entries.principle: Legal and property records built on a doctrine that subsumed the married woman's legal person file her under a man, so her independent action is obscured at the level of the record's structure. She surfaces chiefly as widow, defendant or witness.
entries.example: Under English common-law coverture a wife's legal identity was absorbed into her husband's, so that across centuries of deeds and suits women appear at the margins of transactions conducted in a man's name.
entries.application: To recover a woman's agency from such a record, read the moments when the doctrine failed to contain her, the widowhood, the lawsuit, the will, and reconstruct the rest from the shape of the silence the law imposed.

entries.name: The Recent Record Fails Too
entries.description: Documentary silence reaches into living memory; no record is automatically safe.
entries.principle: Documentary silence is not only an ancient problem; it reaches into living memory, where a mass-market object that a person can still hold can already be beyond bibliographic recovery. The recent gap is often more startling than the antique one, and it teaches that no record is automatically safe.
entries.example: Anne Mather's Caroline (1965), a mainstream genre novel barely sixty years old, has a first-edition publisher and format that reference sources cannot agree on, giving two incompatible answers in a single paragraph.
entries.application: Do not assume the twentieth-century record is complete because it is recent; when your book turns on a modern document, chase the artefact itself rather than trusting the consensus of secondary sources that may all be copying one error.

entries.name: In the Archive Is Not the Same as True
entries.description: In the archive is not the same as true; a document certifies only that a claim was made and kept.
entries.principle: A document is a claim made by whoever produced it, not a transparent window onto events, so its presence in an archive certifies only that the claim was made and kept. The provenance of the claim is the first thing to establish, not the last.
entries.example: The persistence of marketing copy calling Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca a National Book Award winner, when the 1938 honour was a booksellers' poll and the National Book Award was founded in 1950, shows how a false claim survives simply by being repeated in print.
entries.application: For every load-bearing fact, trace it back to the artefact that first asserts it, and never let a claim's mere presence in the record stand in for confirmation of what it asserts.

entries.name: A Source Is Not a Citation of One
entries.description: A source is not a citation of one; copies, editions and translations each add error or agenda.
entries.principle: Between the reader and the original artefact stand transcriptions, edited editions, translations, and summaries of summaries, and each layer can introduce error or agenda. Consensus among secondary sources is not independent confirmation when they are copying one another.
entries.example: The propagation of a single mis-transcribed fact across a dozen reference works, each apparently confirming the others, is a pattern this build has met repeatedly, from mislabelled awards to garbled first-edition dates.
entries.application: Count the layers between your fact and the artefact, and where every source traces to one intermediary, treat the fact as single-sourced no matter how many places repeat it.

entries.name: Every Document Lies in a Characteristic Direction
entries.description: Every document lies toward its purpose, so its genre predicts its characteristic bias.
entries.principle: A document made for a purpose distorts toward that purpose, so its genre predicts its bias. A tax roll undercounts, a confession under torture reports the interrogator's categories, a hagiography exists to prove sanctity, a chronicle flatters its patron, and a petition exaggerates to move a magistrate.
entries.example: A muster roll and a saint's life describe overlapping worlds in incompatible registers, one built to conscript and the other to canonise, and each is trustworthy only about the thing it was made to do.
entries.application: Name a source's purpose before you use it, then trust it about what it was built to record and discount it exactly where its purpose would bend the truth.

entries.name: Read With the Grain and Against It
entries.description: Read a biased source with the grain for its makers' concerns, against it for the suppressed reality.
entries.principle: A biased source is still evidence, read correctly. With the grain it reveals what its makers cared about; against the grain it lets a suppressed reality show through the gaps and contradictions the makers did not intend.
entries.example: A runaway-slave advertisement, written to recapture a person and reduce them to a description, is against its own grain the fullest physical and biographical record of an enslaved individual that often survives.
entries.application: For a hostile or self-interested source, extract the intended message once, then read it a second time for what it inadvertently discloses about the people it was trying to control or erase.

entries.name: Diplomatics: A Genuine Document Has a Knowable Form
entries.description: Diplomatics: a genuine document has a knowable form that can test whether it is authentic.
entries.principle: The authentic document of a period has a describable shape, in its formulae, its script, its seals and its internal structure, and that form can be used to test whether a source is genuine, forged or interpolated. Form is evidence.
entries.example: Jean Mabillon founded the discipline with De re diplomatica (1681), written to settle whether disputed Merovingian charters were forgeries by analysing the conventions a real charter of the age would obey.
entries.application: If a character in your book forges, reads or relies on a document, let them attend to its form as a period reader would, and if you invent a document, know that it has a shape a knowledgeable eye could check.

entries.name: Palaeography Is Slow, Contestable Labour
entries.description: Palaeography is slow, contestable labour; reading the archive is not scanning printed text.
entries.principle: Reading old handwriting is skilled, uncertain work: scripts are period- and region-specific, abbreviation systems are dense, and a damaged word or an ambiguous stroke can change a reading. The person who reads the archive is not scanning printed text.
entries.example: A single ambiguous minim or an expanded abbreviation in a secretary hand can turn one name into another, so that a document's meaning is reconstructed rather than simply read off the page.
entries.application: When your novel stages an act of reading a manuscript, make it the slow, fallible, expert task it was, and let a contested reading become a plot possibility rather than assuming the past arrives legibly.

entries.name: The Confession Under Torture
entries.description: A confession under torture reports the interrogator's categories, not the speaker's beliefs.
entries.principle: A statement extracted under duress is evidence of what the interrogator wanted to hear and of the categories the interrogator imposed, not a transparent report of the speaker's beliefs. Its content is co-authored by the apparatus that produced it.
entries.example: Inquisition and criminal records across early-modern Europe preserve testimony shaped entirely by the questions asked and the danger of certain answers, so the accused speaks always inside a frame designed to convict.
entries.application: Never quote a coerced statement as if it were free first-person speech; dramatise instead the gap between what the record forced a person to say and what the record's own pressure makes visible underneath.

entries.name: The Voice That Survives Only Inside the Apparatus
entries.description: Sometimes a voice survives only inside the very apparatus that destroyed the speaker.
entries.principle: Sometimes an ordinary person's inner world reaches us solely because an institution prosecuted them, so the record that preserves the voice is the same record that destroyed the speaker. The survival is real and the mediation is total.
entries.example: Carlo Ginzburg's The Cheese and the Worms (Italian 1976, English 1980) reconstructs the cosmology of the miller Domenico Scandella, called Menocchio, from the Roman Inquisition trial that condemned him and had him burned around 1599.
entries.application: Where your character's only trace is the file of the power that broke them, build the interior from that hostile document while keeping visible that everything you know arrives through the mechanism that silenced them.

entries.name: Montaillou and the Filtered Peasant Voice
entries.description: Montaillou: even the richest peasant testimony is always a peasant answering an interrogator.
entries.principle: Even the richest surviving testimony of the undocumented is filtered through an interrogator's questions, a notary's Latin and the power differential of a tribunal, so what looks like a peasant speaking is always a peasant answering. The mediation shapes the content, not just its language.
entries.example: Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie's Montaillou (1975) reconstructs a whole Occitan village from the inquisition register of Bishop Jacques Fournier, whose interrogations of suspected Cathars produced the only detailed record of their daily lives.
entries.application: When you borrow such testimony, remember it answers questions you cannot see, and reconstruct the villagers' world knowing that what they volunteered and what they concealed were both governed by the danger of the room.

entries.name: The Mediated Voice
entries.description: A recorded voice is co-authored by whoever recorded, edited and interpreted it.
entries.principle: A recorded voice is co-authored by whoever recorded it, so the abolitionist's editing, the interviewer's framing, and the interpreter's choices are all present in the words attributed to the speaker. The recording purpose leaves fingerprints on the testimony.
entries.example: Nineteenth-century slave narratives shaped for abolitionist audiences, and later as-told-to testimonies mediated by an interviewer, carry the recorder's aims inside the first-person voice they present as unmediated.
entries.application: Treat any transcribed or translated testimony as jointly authored, and where your book relies on such a voice, decide how much of what it says was permitted, prompted or shaped by the person holding the pen.

entries.name: Transmission: The Archetype No Longer Exists
entries.description: Transmission: the archetype is gone, so the text is an inference from its surviving descendants.
entries.principle: Many texts survive only through a chain of copies, the earliest often centuries after composition, so what scholars work from is a reconstruction of a lost original rather than the original itself. The text is an inference from its descendants.
entries.example: Classical works reach us through medieval manuscript traditions in which stemmatic criticism reconstructs an archetype that has not physically survived, assembling the probable original from the pattern of errors its copies share.
entries.application: When a character consults an ancient text, remember they hold a copy of a copy with its own accumulated errors, and let the instability of transmission be a resource rather than a fact you quietly smooth away.

entries.name: Translation Is Interpretation
entries.description: Translation is interpretation; one word choice can smuggle a modern concept into an ancient mouth.
entries.principle: Rendering a source into another language is an act of interpretation, and a single word choice for a legal, kinship or religious term can smuggle a modern concept into an ancient mouth. The translation decides part of the meaning it claims only to convey.
entries.example: Translating a period term for a social relation, an office or an emotion into its nearest modern word can silently import assumptions the original did not hold, so the reader meets the translator's concept believing it to be the source's.
entries.application: Where a translated term is load-bearing for your period's mentality, learn what the original word did and did not mean, and resist letting the convenient modern equivalent think for your characters.

entries.name: The Forged and Interpolated Document
entries.description: Forgery and interpolation, exposed by anachronism in language or form regardless of long belief.
entries.principle: Documents are sometimes forged or altered, and internal evidence, especially anachronism in language or form, can overturn a source's authority regardless of how long it was believed. The exposure is itself a historical act with consequences.
entries.example: Lorenzo Valla demonstrated in 1440 that the Donation of Constantine was a forgery, using philological evidence that its Latin belonged to a later age than it claimed, and in doing so undid a document that had underwritten papal territorial claims.
entries.application: Let a contested or forged document drive your plot as it drove real history, and if a character authenticates or debunks a source, ground the judgement in the period's own tests of form and language rather than modern hindsight.

entries.name: The Distribution of Silence Is Not Random
entries.description: Silence falls hardest on the enslaved, colonized, women and illiterate poor — a pattern of power.
entries.principle: Whose life goes undocumented follows a pattern: silence falls hardest on the enslaved, the colonized, women and the illiterate poor, exactly the people a state's record-making apparatus was not built to see. The gap is structured by power, so writing into it blindly repeats the structure.
entries.example: The plantation, the colonial census and the common-law court each record the same populations as property, subjects or dependents, so their absence as full persons is consistent across otherwise unrelated archives.
entries.application: Map who your period's records were built to see before you decide what you can know, and treat a silenced group's absence as a designed feature of the archive rather than a licence to invent them freely.

entries.name: Critical Fabulation
entries.description: Critical fabulation: narrate the impossible story while marking its impossibility, not filling it.
entries.principle: For lives that survive only as a line in a ledger or a number in an inventory, there is a disciplined way to write: strain against the archive's limits and narrate the impossible story while marking its impossibility, rather than filling the silence with invented interiority that would repeat the violence of reducing a person to a datum.
entries.example: Saidiya Hartman's essay Venus in Two Acts (2008) names this method critical fabulation, developed around the recurring nameless dead girl of the Atlantic slave-trade record.
entries.application: Where the record gives you only a name or a number, write toward the person while keeping the limit visible, and refuse the false comfort of a fully imagined inner life the archive cannot support.

entries.name: Write Around a Gap Without Inventing Into It
entries.description: Write around a gap by implying the undocumented centre through its documented surround.
entries.principle: There is a difference between building a scene around a documented absence and manufacturing the absent content, and the craft lies in implying the undocumented centre through the documented surround rather than asserting what cannot be known.
entries.example: A novel that renders an enslaved person's world through the fully recorded machinery around them, the ship, the ledger, the auction, can make the silenced life present without pretending to a testimony that does not exist.
entries.application: When you cannot know a person's interior, construct the reader's sense of it from the documented world pressing in on all sides, so the centre is felt as a shape defined by its surroundings.

entries.name: Record a Gap as a Gap
entries.description: Record a gap as a gap; naming the silence can teach more than seamlessly filling it.
entries.principle: Sometimes the honest and most powerful move is to name the silence itself, to let the reader feel that the record stops here and that the stopping is the subject. A gap acknowledged teaches more than a gap seamlessly filled.
entries.example: Fiction that stages its own reaching toward an unrecoverable figure, and admits where the reaching fails, turns the archive's limit into meaning rather than hiding it behind confident invention.
entries.application: Consider making the boundary of the record visible on the page, so that the reader knows where knowledge ends and imagination begins, and the silence becomes an argument about what was allowed to be lost.

entries.name: The Enslaved in the Plantation Record
entries.description: The enslaved appear as property, described precisely because made to price, bequeath or recapture them.
entries.principle: Enslaved people appear in the archive as property, in inventories, wills, ship manifests and advertisements, so the fullest surviving description of an individual often exists precisely because it was made to price, bequeath or recapture them. The record's purpose is the violence.
entries.example: A runaway advertisement, composed to return a person to bondage, frequently preserves the most detailed physical and biographical account of an enslaved individual that survives at all.
entries.application: Read these documents against their grain for the person they were made to control, and build from them without ever forgetting, or letting the reader forget, the purpose that produced the only trace.

entries.name: Reasoning Openly Across the Gap
entries.description: Cross an evidentiary gap openly, marking inference as inference — the disciplined 'perhaps'.
entries.principle: A historian can cross an evidentiary gap honestly by saying where the record stops and marking inference as inference, the "perhaps" that separates what is known from what is reconstructed. The declared boundary is what keeps the reconstruction disciplined.
entries.example: Natalie Zemon Davis's The Return of Martin Guerre (1983) openly signals where the sixteenth-century record ends and where she supplies probability about the impostor and the wife who may have known, keeping the seam visible.
entries.application: Adopt the historian's discipline of marking your own inferences, at least for yourself, so you always know which parts of your reconstruction the record supports and which parts you have supplied.

entries.name: The Line Between Inference and Invention
entries.description: Where reasoned inference becomes invention is contested; the novelist works the line the historian argues.
entries.principle: Exactly where reasoned inference becomes unwarranted invention is genuinely contested, and the dispute is instructive rather than resolvable. The novelist works on the same line the historian argues over, with more freedom and the same obligation to know when it is crossed.
entries.example: Robert Finlay's 1988 critique of Davis's Martin Guerre charged that she had crossed from evidence into invention in imagining the wife's complicity, a documented disagreement about the precise boundary the historian must manage; the field has not settled it and this card takes no side.
entries.application: Study a real dispute of this kind before drafting your own gap-crossings, and decide consciously, scene by scene, whether you are inferring from evidence or inventing beyond it, since the reader's trust depends on the difference.

entries.name: Oral Tradition Is a Different Record, Not an Absent One
entries.description: Oral tradition is a different record, not an absent one, held elsewhere and maybe not yours to take.
entries.principle: When the written archive is silent about a community, the conclusion that there is no record is frequently false; the record exists in oral form, with its own custodians, transmission rules and authority claims, and it is held elsewhere and may not be the writer's to take.
entries.example: The West African epic of Sundiata, maintained and performed by griots as trained custodians, and Jan Vansina's Oral Tradition as History (1985), together establish that oral tradition can be interrogated as a source with its own source-criticism rather than dismissed as folklore.
entries.application: Before writing "there was no record," ask who holds the memory, in what form and by what authority, and treat a living oral tradition as a source to be approached with its custodians rather than a vacancy to fill.

entries.name: The Failure Modes of Oral Tradition
entries.description: Oral tradition's failure modes — telescoping, reshaping to present need — are the condition of using it.
entries.principle: Oral tradition is a record with characteristic distortions distinct from the archive's: it telescopes chronology, drops what a present generation has no use for, and reshapes toward current needs. Knowing its failure modes is the condition of using it well, not a reason to discount it.
entries.example: The argument by Patrick Nunn and Nicholas Reid that some Aboriginal Australian oral traditions encode coastal changes from post-glacial sea-level rise thousands of years old is serious and genuinely contested; it is presented here as argued rather than established, precisely because oral transmission's reach over deep time is disputed.
entries.application: Interrogate an oral source with the same rigour you bring to a document, allowing for its own patterns of compression and adaptation, and where scholars dispute how far it can reach, let your book hold the uncertainty rather than resolve it.

entries.name: Who May Speak a Tradition
entries.description: Traditions carry rules on who may tell them, to whom and when; access is not permission.
entries.principle: Traditions carry authority rules about who may tell them, to whom, and in what setting, so access is not the same as permission. A story freely available to hear may still not be freely available to retell or to fictionalise.
entries.example: In custodial traditions the right to perform a genealogy or a sacred narrative belongs to trained or designated bearers, and a community may withhold or restrict what an outsider is permitted to reproduce.
entries.application: Distinguish what you can find out from what you are entitled to use, and where a tradition is held under rules of authority, seek permission or write around it rather than assuming that discoverability confers a right to publish.

entries.name: Documented Only in the Colonizer's Categories
entries.description: A colonised people recorded only in the colonizer's categories arrives pre-interpreted through an alien frame.
entries.principle: A colonised people is often recorded solely in the colonizer's language and classifications, so even the surviving evidence arrives pre-interpreted through an alien frame. The categories themselves are part of what must be resisted, not just the conclusions.
entries.example: Populations known to the archive only through imperial censuses, tax rolls and criminal ethnographies survive under names, tribes and traits the administrators invented for the convenience of rule.
entries.application: Where your sources are entirely the colonizer's, treat their categories as evidence about the colonizer, and reconstruct the colonised world by asking what those categories were designed to flatten or ignore.

entries.name: The Mark Instead of the Signature
entries.description: The illiterate enter the record through others' writing, signing with a witnessed mark.
entries.principle: The illiterate, who were most people for most of history, enter the record chiefly through others' writing, signing with a mark someone else witnessed. Their literacy, or its absence, shapes what of them could be preserved in their own hand, which is usually nothing.
entries.example: A deposition or contract closed with an X and a clerk's notation preserves a person's assent while erasing their voice, so that agreement survives and expression does not.
entries.application: For a non-literate character, remember that almost nothing they produced in writing can survive, and build their record from what literate others wrote about, to or against them, treating that mediation as the normal condition of their visibility.

entries.name: The Undocumented Centre, Rendered by Implication
entries.description: The undocumented centre rendered by implication; the known frame makes the unknown middle legible.
entries.principle: The hardest scene is one about a person whose interiority the record denies you entirely, and the craft answer is to let the fully documented surrounding world imply the centre rather than asserting it. The known frame makes the unknown middle legible.
entries.example: A chapter that reconstructs the ship, the market, the household and the law around an undocumented life can make that life vivid without inventing a single unsupported thought inside it.
entries.application: Build outward-in: research the documented world that pressed on your silenced subject until it is dense enough that the reader infers the person at its centre, and let that inference do the work invention would have done dishonestly.

entries.name: The Non-Textual Record Is an Equal Partner
entries.description: The non-textual record is an equal witness, each method with its own confidence and failure modes.
entries.principle: When the written sources are absent or lying, material evidence carries the history, and archaeology, climate science, osteology, genetics and the rest are not illustrations of the text but independent witnesses with their own authority. Each also has its own confidence levels and failure modes, which must be stated as plainly as its findings.
entries.example: For most of the human past there is no text at all, and what is known comes from stratigraphy, bone, pollen and isotope, so the non-textual record is not a supplement to history but often the whole of it.
entries.application: Treat physical evidence as a full partner to the document, and whenever your book leans on a scientific finding about the past, carry its uncertainty onto the page as faithfully as its result.

entries.name: Archaeology Gives Sequence, Not Motive
entries.description: Archaeology gives sequence, not motive, and over-represents durable goods over the organic majority.
entries.principle: Excavation reveals sequence, activity and construction through the law of superposition, but it cannot recover motive, belief, language or names. Its great distortion is survivorship toward durable goods, so the material past over-represents stone, ceramic and metal and loses the organic majority of what people made.
entries.example: The equation of a material assemblage with an ethnic group, the pots-are-not-people problem, has repeatedly misled interpretation, since a shared style of object need not mean a shared people.
entries.application: Use archaeology to fix what happened in what order and what was done where, but do not let it supply the beliefs, speech or intentions it cannot recover, and remember that what rotted away outnumbered what survived.

entries.name: Dendrochronology: Exact Years, With a Catch
entries.description: Dendrochronology can fix an exact year, with the old-wood and matching-chronology catches.
entries.principle: Where a regional master chronology exists, tree-ring dating can fix a felled timber to the exact year and sometimes the season, the most precise pre-instrumental method there is. Its failure modes are real: it needs enough rings and a matching chronology, and the old-wood problem means a timber can be reused or lose its outer rings, dating the tree's death rather than the building.
entries.example: Timber-framed structures have been dated to a single year by ring-matching, while reused beams and lost sapwood have on occasion made a building look older than it is.
entries.application: If your plot turns on dating a wooden structure, you may legitimately claim year-level precision where a chronology exists, but respect the old-wood caveat rather than assuming a beam's rings date the moment it was raised.

entries.name: Ice Cores and the Deepening Uncertainty
entries.description: Ice cores date eruptions with high resolution near the surface; uncertainty deepens with depth.
entries.principle: Annual layers in ice, counted like tree rings, record climate and volcanic eruptions with high resolution near the surface, and a sulphate spike can date a major eruption. But dating uncertainty grows with depth as layers thin and deform, so an ancient eruption's ice-core date can still carry a multi-year band, and such attributions are actively revised.
entries.example: The mid-sixth-century dust-veil events around 536 to 540, which darkened skies across the northern hemisphere, have been tied to volcanic signals in the cores and repeatedly re-dated as the science improves, illustrating that even a dramatic climate marker carries revision risk.
entries.application: Treat an ice-core date for a distant event as a range under revision, not a fixed year, and if a character lives through a volcanic winter, let the science's own uncertainty inform how definite you allow the narrative to be.

entries.name: Radiocarbon Gives a Range, Not a Date
entries.description: Radiocarbon returns a calibrated range, not a date, with reservoir, contamination and plateau limits.
entries.principle: Radiocarbon dating of organics returns a calibrated probability range, not a point, and two-sigma ranges can span a century or more. Its failure modes include the reservoir effect, by which aquatic organisms date too old, contamination, and calibration plateaus where wide ranges are irreducible.
entries.example: On a calibration plateau such as the earlier first millennium BCE, a sample can only be placed within a broad band no matter how careful the measurement, so the method's precision is bounded by the curve itself.
entries.application: Never let a character declare that carbon dating proved an exact year; write the result as the probability range it is, and let the reservoir and plateau problems be available complications rather than errors to hide.

entries.name: Osteology and the Osteological Paradox
entries.description: Osteology reads the body, but a sample of the dead may misrepresent the living.
entries.principle: Human bone records diet, disease, healed trauma, age, biological sex, mobility and interpersonal violence, but it is distorted by preservation and by a subtler trap: a sample of the dead may misrepresent the living, because those who died young may have been either the frailest or the robust who succumbed fast. Sexing juveniles is unreliable, and biological sex from bone is not gender in life.
entries.example: The osteological paradox, named by Wood and colleagues in 1992, warns that a cemetery population's apparent health cannot be read straight off as the health of the community that produced it.
entries.application: Use skeletal evidence for what a body plainly shows, a healed fracture, a childhood spent elsewhere, a violent death, but resist turning a graveyard's dead into a portrait of the living, and keep biological findings distinct from the social roles a novel must imagine.

entries.name: Ancient DNA: Powerful for Populations, Silent on the Person
entries.description: Ancient DNA is powerful for populations, near-silent on the person, and dangerous read as identity.
entries.principle: Ancient DNA has rewritten prehistory at the scale of populations and migrations, but it is near-useless for the individual life a novel narrates, and it is dangerous when read as identity. The interpretive step from a genetic signal to a mechanism, or from ancestry to ethnicity, language or peoplehood, is genuinely contested and must be flagged, not asserted.
entries.example: The finding that Neolithic Britain's gene pool was largely replaced within centuries of the Bell Beaker arrival, reported by Olalde and colleagues in Nature in 2018, is a solid population result; whether "replacement" implies violence, disease or differential fertility, and whether steppe ancestry maps onto any people or language, remains disputed.
entries.application: Draw on genetics for broad movements of populations if your canvas is wide, but never let it decide a character's identity or ethnicity, and where you invoke it, carry the scholarly dispute about mechanism and meaning rather than the headline certainty.

entries.name: Environmental History: Stressor, Not Destiny
entries.description: Environment is a stressor mediated by society, not destiny; the failure is climate determinism.
entries.principle: Climate and environment are historical actors, but as stressors mediated by politics and society, not as direct causes. The failure mode is climate determinism, reading a cold decade as the cause of a war when it is at most a pressure a society may or may not absorb.
entries.example: Geoffrey Parker's Global Crisis (2013) ties the upheavals of the seventeenth century to the Little Ice Age while insisting that climate acted through human institutions, so that the same cooling produced collapse in some polities and resilience in others.
entries.application: Let weather and harvest press on your period, but route their effects through the specific society's capacity to cope, and resist the neat story in which a climate event simply causes a human catastrophe.

entries.name: Numismatics: Coins as Chronology and Propaganda
entries.description: Coins date a deposit and broadcast an official self-image; the portrait is aspiration, not reportage.
entries.principle: Coins date a sealed deposit as no older than their latest specimen, track the economy through debasement, map the reach of an authority, and broadcast an official self-image. Their failure modes: coins circulate for decades, so they fix the earliest possible closing rather than the event, hoards over-represent crisis, and the imperial portrait is aspiration, not reportage.
entries.example: A hoard's latest coin gives a terminus post quem for its burial, falling silver content measures fiscal stress, and an emperor's chosen face on the coinage is chosen propaganda rather than a likeness.
entries.application: Use coins to bound your chronology and to read a regime's self-presentation, but remember a buried hoard usually marks a moment of fear and loss, and the ruler's coin-face tells you what he wished to project, not what he looked like or did.

entries.name: Historical Linguistics: A Proto-Language Is Not a Proto-People
entries.description: A reconstructed proto-language is not a proto-people; the slide to race and invasion is catastrophic.
entries.principle: The comparative method reconstructs unattested parent languages from systematic sound correspondences, and loanwords and place-names preserve vanished contacts, but reconstructing a proto-language does not reconstruct a proto-people. The catastrophic failure mode is the slide from a language family to a race to an invasion.
entries.example: The nineteenth- and twentieth-century move from "Indo-European languages" to an "Aryan race" and an "Aryan invasion" ideology shows how a linguistic reconstruction was turned into a racial myth, when a language can spread by elite dominance or trade without mass migration.
entries.application: Use linguistic evidence for contact, borrowing and the survival of lost tongues in names, but never equate a language with a people or a genome, and treat any story of a language arriving by conquest as a claim to be tested, not assumed.

entries.name: Iconography: Convention Before Observation
entries.description: Iconography follows convention before observation, so a realistic-looking detail may be a symbol.
entries.principle: Images encode dress, ritual, technology and hierarchy, and what a society wished to depict, but they follow iconographic convention rather than life-drawing, so a realistic-looking detail may be a symbol. Patrons' agendas flatter, and the elite's commissioned art survives over the ordinary.
entries.example: The Bayeux Tapestry is at once near-contemporary testimony to the events of 1066 and a partisan Norman narrative of them, so its images inform and argue in the same stitches.
entries.application: Read a period image for what its conventions permitted and its patron wanted, extract the incidental detail its makers did not think to falsify, and never treat a later or foreign artist's depiction of a scene as an eyewitness record.

entries.name: Experimental Archaeology
entries.description: Experimental archaeology tests whether a technique actually works, establishing feasibility.
entries.principle: Reconstructing a technique or a structure and testing whether it actually works can establish feasibility that no document confirms, turning speculation about how something was done into demonstrable possibility or impossibility.
entries.example: Rebuilding an ancient boat, kiln or tool and putting it to use has repeatedly shown which reconstructions are viable and which are not, supplying evidence the written and material records leave open.
entries.application: When your plot depends on whether a period process was possible in the time available, look to experimental reconstruction for a feasibility check, and let a technique's real constraints, not convenience, govern what your characters can achieve.

entries.name: Zooarchaeology
entries.description: Zooarchaeology reads animal bone for the everyday economy the documents rarely describe.
entries.principle: Animal bone from a site records husbandry, hunting, butchery and diet, revealing what a community raised, killed and ate, and how they managed the animals they depended on. It reconstructs an everyday economy the documents rarely describe.
entries.example: The mix of species, ages at slaughter and butchery marks in a settlement's animal remains can distinguish a herding economy from a hunting one and show whether stock was kept for meat, milk or traction.
entries.application: Ground your period's foodways and working animals in what the faunal record supports rather than in generic pastoral imagery, and let the real balance of herd and hunt shape the texture of daily life.

entries.name: Palynology
entries.description: Palynology tracks vegetation and land-use, making the landscape itself a dated document.
entries.principle: Preserved pollen records vegetation and its change over time, tracking clearance, cultivation and abandonment, so the landscape itself becomes a dated document of human land-use. It reveals environmental history at a resolution no chronicle offers.
entries.example: A pollen sequence showing forest giving way to cereal and pasture, then reverting, can date an episode of settlement and its collapse without a single written word.
entries.application: Let the worked landscape of your period rest on what pollen and land-use evidence indicate about clearance and cultivation, so that the countryside your characters move through is the one the science reconstructs rather than a timeless backdrop.

entries.name: Provenance by Isotope and Metallurgy
entries.description: Isotope and metallurgy source materials to their origins, revealing trade invisible in any text.
entries.principle: Isotopic and compositional analysis can source metal, stone and other materials to their origins, revealing trade networks and long-distance contact invisible in any text. The object's chemistry carries its own itinerary.
entries.example: Sourcing the metal in an artefact or the stone in a monument to a distant deposit can demonstrate exchange across regions that no document records, redrawing the map of a period's connections.
entries.application: Use provenance evidence to establish who was really connected to whom, and let a traded material's true origin, rather than assumption, tell you how far your period's world extended.

entries.name: Underwater Archaeology
entries.description: A shipwreck is a sealed time-capsule, a working world preserved at the instant it went down.
entries.principle: A shipwreck is a sealed time-capsule, a single moment's cargo, tools and lives preserved together on the seabed, giving a cross-section of a working world at the instant it went down. Such sites can hold organic material that land sites lose.
entries.example: An excavated wreck can preserve a whole ship's contents as a coherent assemblage, so that trade goods, personal possessions and shipboard equipment are found in the relationship they held at the moment of sinking.
entries.application: If your story touches seafaring or trade, treat a wreck-derived assemblage as a uniquely intact snapshot, and build the ship's social and material world from the coherence such a site preserves.

entries.name: The Confidence Level Is the Point
entries.description: The confidence level is the point: a date is a range, a signal an inference, a reconstruction a probability.
entries.principle: Every non-textual method carries an error bar, and stating it is not a hedge but the substance of using the evidence honestly. A date is a range, a signal is an inference, and a reconstruction is a probability, so the discipline is to know and convey how firmly each finding is held.
entries.example: A radiocarbon range, an ice-core band, a contested genetic mechanism and a convention-bound image each come with a different degree of certainty, and collapsing them all into flat fact misrepresents the past as better known than it is.
entries.application: For every scientific claim your book makes about the past, know its confidence level and let the narrative's certainty match the evidence's, so the reader is never told the record is firmer than it actually is.

entries.name: The Settled Narrative Is Provisional
entries.description: The settled narrative is provisional; a history is a report from a moment, and the moment moves.
entries.principle: What a period "knows" about its past is a current state, not a final one, and later evidence or a later question can overturn it. A history is a report from a moment, and the moment moves.
entries.example: Accounts of the same event written in 1950 and in 2020 routinely differ not because the event changed but because the archive was re-read, new evidence arrived, or the questions historians thought worth asking shifted.
entries.application: Treat the standard account your book relies on as revisable, and where you can, dramatise history as something being argued over rather than a fixed backdrop the characters inhabit.

entries.name: The Winner's History and Its Correction
entries.description: The winner's history can dominate for generations until corrected, the correction its own event.
entries.principle: A narrative written by the victors can dominate for generations before being corrected, and the correction is itself a historical event, driven by whose questions finally count. The same evidence yields opposite stories depending on who is permitted to interpret it.
entries.example: The early-twentieth-century Dunning School cast American Reconstruction as a corrupt failure; W. E. B. Du Bois dissented in Black Reconstruction in America (1935) and was marginalised, and only by the time of Eric Foner's Reconstruction (1988) had the field inverted to something near his view.
entries.application: Identify whose account of your period became standard and why, and consider writing from the vantage the winning narrative suppressed, treating the dominant version as a claim to be tested rather than the truth to be dramatised.

entries.name: The Body Against the Propaganda Portrait
entries.description: The body against the propaganda portrait: physical remains can break a myth the documents preserved.
entries.principle: Physical remains can adjudicate between a partisan story and the fact, settling by evidence what a hostile narrative had closed. The record of the body is not immune to interpretation, but it can break a myth the documents alone preserved.
