entries.example: The remains of Richard III, found beneath a Leicester car park in 2012 and identified in 2013 through skeletal trauma, radiocarbon and a mitochondrial-DNA match to a maternal-line descendant, confirmed a real scoliosis rather than the Tudor propaganda hunchback and showed how he died.
entries.application: Where a reputation rests on a hostile portrait, ask whether physical evidence exists to test it, and let a novel exploit the gap between what a regime said of its enemy and what the enemy's own body reveals.

entries.name: When the Record Vindicates the Testimony
entries.description: Sometimes oral memory holds what the archive suppressed, later confirmed by documentary or forensic work.
entries.principle: Sometimes oral memory holds an event the official record actively suppressed, and later documentary or forensic work confirms what the archive denied. The community's memory was the accurate record, and the archive was the falsification.
entries.example: The Tulsa Race Massacre of 1921 was long minimised in official accounts, while descendants preserved the memory, and twenty-first-century commissions and mass-grave excavation from 2020 onward have begun recovering forensically what the record had erased.
entries.application: When your subject is an event a community remembers and the official record diminishes, treat the oral memory as potentially the truer source, and let the collision between suppressed record and living testimony be part of the story.

entries.name: A New Method Delivers a Precision the Old Record Could Not
entries.description: A new method can deliver a precision the old record could not, closing a centuries-open question.
entries.principle: A technical advance can fix with sudden exactness what the documentary record left vague, so that a question open for centuries is closed by a method no earlier historian possessed. The past does not change, but the precision with which it can be known does.
entries.example: The Norse presence at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, excavated in the 1960s, was pinned to the exact year 1021 by a 2021 study that read a known cosmic-ray event in the rings of felled timber, dating pre-Columbian transatlantic contact to a firm year.
entries.application: Let a period's own limits of dating stand where they stood, but remember that certainty about the past is a moving frontier, and a fact vague in one generation can become exact in the next.

entries.name: Forgery Exposed
entries.description: A forgery can warp a narrative for decades until evidence exposes it, correcting all built on it.
entries.principle: A forgery can warp a narrative for decades before internal or physical evidence exposes it, and the exposure retroactively corrects everything built on the fake. The fraud and its unmasking are both part of the record's history.
entries.example: Piltdown Man distorted the story of human origins for roughly forty years until it was exposed as a composite forgery in 1953, and the Hitler Diaries were accepted by some experts in 1983 before rapid authentication tests destroyed them.
entries.application: A forged document or artefact can drive your plot as it has driven real scholarship, and if a character authenticates or debunks one, ground the test in the period's or the science's actual methods rather than in convenient intuition.

entries.name: The Quantitative Turn Recovered Ordinary Lives
entries.description: The quantitative turn read records in bulk to recover the ordinary lives the political narrative omitted.
entries.principle: Reading tax rolls, parish registers and censuses in bulk let social historians recover the ordinary people the political narrative omitted, converting records made for administration into evidence of lives never meant to be remembered. The method found history in documents made for other purposes.
entries.example: From the 1960s onward, social history built demographic and everyday-life accounts of the poor and obscure by aggregating parish and fiscal records, recovering populations the great-man narrative had left out.
entries.application: Where no one wrote about your characters directly, look to the administrative record in aggregate for the shape of their lives, and let the bulk data of births, prices and burials reconstruct what no individual document preserves.

entries.name: Date Your Secondary Sources
entries.description: Date your secondary sources; an old standard history can import a superseded account as current fact.
entries.principle: A secondary source carries the moment it was written, and a mid-century standard history may rest on a consensus since overturned. Using an authoritative-looking book without knowing its date can import a superseded account as if it were current fact.
entries.example: A respected general history from one era can confidently state as settled what later evidence reversed, so its authority is real about its own moment and unreliable about the present state of knowledge.
entries.application: Note when each secondary source was written and check whether its field has moved since, so your reconstruction rests on the current understanding rather than on a confident book whose consensus has quietly collapsed.

entries.category: The Novelist's Contract with the Record
entries.name: The Author's Note as a Contract
entries.description: The author's note is a contract declaring what was changed, compressed and invented.
entries.principle: The author's note is where invention is declared: what was changed, compressed, invented and where the book departs from the record. It is a contract with the reader about the boundary between the found and the made, and its honesty underwrites the book's authority.
entries.example: A note that states plainly which characters are real, which events are documented and where the author has imagined lets the reader trust the rest, because the seam between record and invention has been shown rather than hidden.
entries.application: Decide what your note must disclose so a reader knows which parts of your book are answerable to the record, and treat that disclosure as part of the work rather than an afterthought appended to it.

entries.category: The Novelist's Contract with the Record
entries.name: Fill the Gap, Do Not Move the Furniture
entries.description: Fill the gap, don't move the furniture: imagine into blanks without contradicting the documented record.
entries.principle: The historical novelist can imagine freely into what the record leaves blank, motive, private conversation, interior life, while not knowingly contradicting what the record establishes, the documented dates, deaths and acts. Facts are not truth, though they are part of it, and the craft is to supply the truth the facts cannot reach without falsifying the facts themselves.
entries.example: Hilary Mantel's Cromwell novels, beginning with Wolf Hall (2009), fill Thomas Cromwell's undocumented interior in exhaustive detail while leaving the documented furniture of events exactly where the record places it.
entries.application: Mark the fixed points of your period, the things genuinely known, then invent only in the spaces between them, so your reconstruction adds interior truth without moving a single documented fact.

entries.category: The Novelist's Contract with the Record
entries.name: The Declared Departure
entries.description: The declared departure marks where the object ends and invention begins, licensing the freedom around it.
entries.principle: A novel can be built from a documented fragment and openly mark where the object ends and invention begins, so the reader always knows the ratio of found to made. The declaration is what licenses the imaginative freedom around it.
entries.example: Geraldine Brooks builds fiction from real historical seeds and signals the departures in her afterwords, as with the self-quarantined plague village of Eyam behind Year of Wonders (2001) and the absent father of Little Women reimagined against the Civil War in March (2005).
entries.application: When your book grows from a real object, event or person, tell the reader where the documented seed stops and your invention begins, and let that candour be the ground on which the invention stands.

entries.category: The Novelist's Contract with the Record
entries.name: Gap Filled Versus Record Contradicted
entries.description: Filling a gap versus contradicting the record: both can be legitimate, but contradiction must be declared.
entries.principle: Inventing a conversation on a day two documented people are known to have met fills a gap; placing a person where the record puts them elsewhere, or having them survive a death the record dates, contradicts the record. Both can be legitimate, but contradiction is a different act that must be declared rather than smuggled.
entries.example: The counterfactual and alternate-history modes contradict the record deliberately and openly, which is honest, whereas a book that quietly moves a documented event to suit its plot while implying fidelity has broken the contract.
entries.application: Know at every turn whether you are filling a gap or contradicting the record, and if you contradict it, do so on purpose and in the open, never by hoping the reader will not notice.

entries.category: The Novelist's Contract with the Record
entries.name: What Is Owed to a Living Tradition
entries.description: A living tradition has custodians with a stake; taking it to fictionalise can be extraction, not research.
entries.principle: A dead archive has no living claimant, but a living tradition, an oral history a community still holds, a sacred narrative, a still-mourned recent atrocity, has custodians with a stake and sometimes a right of refusal. There is no record is often false, and taking what belongs to a living people to fictionalise can be extraction rather than research.
entries.example: Where a community holds its own history in trust, mining it for a novel without its custodians treats a living inheritance as raw material, which is a different act from working an ownerless archive of Roman tax rolls.
entries.application: Establish whether the past you are using is held by living people, and if it is, research it with its custodians or write around it, rather than extracting a story that was never yours to take.

entries.category: The Novelist's Contract with the Record
entries.name: The Documentary Overclaim and Its Inverse
entries.description: Two opposite overclaims borrow the record's credibility without paying its price.
entries.principle: Two opposite dishonesties threaten the form: the based-on-a-true-story overclaim, which asserts documentary authority for what is largely invented, and its inverse, a book that invents heavily while implying the research backs it. Both borrow the record's credibility without paying its price.
entries.example: A novel that trumpets its factual basis while altering the substance, or one whose apparatus of dates and sources implies a fidelity the story does not honour, exploits the reader's trust in the record while betraying it.
entries.application: Match your claims to your practice: if you invent freely, do not dress the book as documentary, and if you assert fidelity, earn it, so the reader's trust is placed where the work actually stands.

entries.category: The Novelist's Contract with the Record
entries.name: Depicting Atrocity
entries.description: Depicting atrocity: a claim about people whose descendants live, named plainly and analysed as craft.
entries.principle: When the material is slavery, genocide, colonial violence or occupation, the historical question is what kind of claim the book makes about people whose descendants are alive, and what it is prepared to answer for. The subject is in scope, named plainly and analysed as craft, neither censored nor relished, and the failure is to use catastrophe as a backdrop for uplift.
entries.example: A book that carries both the documented failures of the genre and the legitimate artistic uses of such material teaches method rather than avoidance, whereas one that stages suffering for the reader's comfort borrows a gravity it has not earned.
entries.application: Before using an atrocity as material, decide what you are asserting about the real people it happened to, build the book to answer for that claim, and keep the depiction analytical and answerable rather than either sanitised or savoured.

entries.category: The Novelist's Contract with the Record
entries.name: The Bibliography Note
entries.description: The bibliography note shows the research without claiming the invention is itself research.
entries.principle: Some novelists append a list of sources, declaring the research base without claiming that the invention is itself research. The bibliography shows the work behind the book while keeping the line between what was studied and what was imagined intact.
entries.example: A closing note that names the histories, archives and testimonies consulted lets a reader pursue the real record and gauge the depth of preparation, without implying that the novel's invented scenes are documented.
entries.application: Consider naming your principal sources so the reader can follow them, and word the note so it credits the research without converting your imaginative choices into false claims of evidence.

entries.name: The Diagnostic Block: What Claim Is This Book Making
entries.description: The diagnostic root: what kind of claim about the past is this book making.
entries.principle: These first twenty Craft cards are the pack's diagnostic block, and they descend not from general novel craft but from the organising claim that historical fiction makes an assertion about the past. Each traces to one of four questions, and the first is the root: what kind of claim is this book making, fidelity, recovery, emotional truth, or deliberate invention against the record, because every later craft decision follows from the answer.
entries.example: Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers (1844) and Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall (2009) sit in the same genre making opposite claims, one frankly inventing for pleasure, the other reconstructing a documented life, and neither is failing at the other's task.
entries.application: Before drafting, state in one sentence what kind of claim your book makes about the past, and treat that sentence as the standard every scene must answer to, since a book that has not decided its claim cannot be held to any.

entries.name: Where the Documented Ends and Invention Begins
entries.description: The second diagnostic: knowing where the documented record stops and necessary invention starts.
entries.principle: The second diagnostic question is where the documented record stops and the necessary invention starts, and the craft is to know the seam even when the reader is not shown it. A novelist who cannot locate that line in their own manuscript has lost track of what they are answerable for.
entries.example: Marguerite Yourcenar's Memoirs of Hadrian (1951) makes the seam its subject, staging the emperor as a dying man reaching across the very gaps the record leaves, so that the boundary between fact and reconstruction is felt rather than hidden.
entries.application: Keep a private account of where you are inventing past the record, so that at every point you know whether you are filling a gap or supplying what the record forbids, and can decide each case on purpose.

entries.name: How the Silence Is Being Handled
entries.description: The third diagnostic: whether a silence is filled, marked as a gap, or a record held elsewhere.
entries.principle: The third diagnostic question is how the book treats what the record does not contain: whether a gap is filled, marked as a gap, or recognised as a record held elsewhere. The handling of silence is a craft decision with an ethics attached, not a technical afterthought.
entries.example: Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987) treats the silence of the slave record not as a blank to be filled with documentary confidence but as a presence to be rendered through testimony and haunting, a deliberate method for the unrecorded.
entries.application: For each silence your book must cross, choose consciously whether to fill it, name it, or leave it to the community that holds it, and let that choice express what kind of claim the book is making rather than defaulting to invention.

entries.name: What Authenticity Actually Requires Here
entries.description: The fourth diagnostic: what this particular book's contract of authenticity actually demands.
entries.principle: The fourth diagnostic question is what the reader's expectation of authenticity actually demands in this particular book, because the requirement is not constant. A swashbuckler and a Holocaust novel owe their readers different things, and mistaking one book's contract for the other's is a craft error.
entries.example: A reader of Bernard Cornwell's Sharpe accepts liberties a reader of a documented-atrocity novel would find intolerable, and each expectation is correct for its book, so authenticity is calibrated to the claim rather than fixed.
entries.application: Identify what your specific reader will require to trust this book, then meet that requirement exactly, neither burdening a light adventure with scholarship it does not need nor granting a grave subject the licence only a lighter one has earned.

entries.name: Anachronism of Fact
entries.description: An object or word out of its time breaks the claim at the level of fact — the most checkable failure.
entries.principle: An object, technology, word or institution placed outside its real time breaks the book's claim on the past at the level of fact, and a single verifiable error can forfeit the reader's trust in everything around it. Factual anachronism is the most checkable failure the genre has.
entries.example: A tomato on a medieval European table, a wristwatch before its invention, or a word coined a century after the scene each snaps the reader out of the reconstruction and invites doubt about the rest.
entries.application: Verify the date of every named object, term and institution against its real first appearance, and treat the research burden as heaviest exactly where a detail feels too ordinary to check.

entries.name: Anachronism of Mind
entries.description: Presentism: importing modern minds into the past, a deeper falsification than any misplaced object.
entries.principle: Harder than factual anachronism is presentism, the importing of modern values, assumptions and sensibilities into people who could not have held them, so that period characters conveniently think as the author's contemporaries do. It flatters the reader and falsifies the past more deeply than any misplaced object.
entries.example: A medieval or ancient character who holds fully modern views on equality, faith or the self reads as a present-day person in costume, and the reconstruction becomes a mirror rather than a window.
entries.application: Establish what your period took for granted that a modern reader would reject, and let characters hold those assumptions without authorial flinching, reserving any modern verdict for the book's structure rather than smuggling it into a character's mind.

entries.name: The Period-Accurate and Repellent Protagonist
entries.description: A period-accurate but repellent protagonist rendered without endorsing or anachronistically redeeming them.
entries.principle: Sometimes the honest reconstruction of a period requires a sympathetic protagonist whose views are accurate to their time and repellent to ours, and the craft problem is to render them truthfully without either endorsing or anachronistically redeeming them. Cleaning up the character to spare the reader is itself a falsification.
entries.example: A slaveholder, a colonial administrator or an inquisitor drawn with full interiority and period-accurate conviction forces the reader to inhabit a worldview the book need not approve, which is a harder and truer act than supplying a modern conscience the person would not have had.
entries.application: When your protagonist's real views are monstrous by present standards, resist giving them an implausible modern enlightenment, and let the book's judgement live in what the story reveals rather than in the character's convenient dissent.

entries.name: The Research-to-Page Ratio
entries.description: The iceberg: research deeply, show a tenth; the failure is displaying the notes as a tour.
entries.principle: What the novelist must know vastly exceeds what the novel should show, and the craft is the iceberg: research deeply enough that the visible tenth rests on a submerged nine. The failure is to display the research, converting a story into a tour of the author's notes.
entries.example: Patrick O'Brian's naval novels rest on exhaustive seamanship yet surface only the fraction a competent crew member would remark on, so the depth is felt as authority rather than paraded as exposition.
entries.application: Research until you could answer questions the book never raises, then put on the page only what a character would notice or the scene requires, and cut any detail present merely to prove you found it.

entries.name: Dialogue Register
entries.description: Period dialogue between forsooth-pastiche and modern slang, aiming at a neutral, timeless register.
entries.principle: Period dialogue must avoid two opposite failures: the pastiche of forsooth-and-prithee that no one ever spoke, and the modern idiom or slang that drops the reader out of the period. The aim is a neutral, timeless register that reads as natural while excluding the anachronistic word.
entries.example: Convincing historical dialogue usually invents a plausible plainness rather than reproducing period speech, screening out modern idiom and recent coinages while declining the mock-antique, so the talk feels neither costumed nor contemporary.
entries.application: Build a register that avoids both fake-old and unmistakably modern diction, check individual words and idioms for anachronistic coinage, and remember you are creating an effect of period speech, not transcribing it.

entries.name: How Characters Know What They Know
entries.description: Information moved at its period's speed; what a character can know, and when, is a hard constraint.
entries.principle: Information moved at the speed of its period, so what a character can know, and when, is a hard constraint the plot must respect. Rumour, letters, riders and ships carried news at rates that shaped every decision, and a plot that leaks modern connectivity into a pre-modern world cheats.
entries.example: A commander acting on intelligence that could not yet have reached him, or a family learning of a distant death faster than any messenger could travel, breaks the period's real information geography.
entries.application: Map how news, orders and knowledge actually travelled in your period, and let the delays, gaps and unreliability of that transmission generate suspense and error rather than being quietly overridden for convenience.

entries.name: Writing a Documented Atrocity
entries.description: A real atrocity handled as craft: named plainly and analysed, neither censored nor made spectacle.
entries.principle: When the material is a real atrocity, the craft question is what kind of claim the book makes about it and what it is prepared to answer for, and the answer is a craft answer rather than a separate ethics apparatus. The subject is named plainly and analysed, neither censored nor turned into spectacle.
entries.example: A novel that carries both the documented failures of the genre and the legitimate uses of such material teaches method, while one that stages suffering to move the reader borrows a gravity it has not earned.
entries.application: Decide what your book asserts about the real people an atrocity happened to, build it to answer for that assertion, and keep the depiction answerable rather than either sanitised into comfort or heightened into thrill.

entries.name: Exposition Without the Tour Guide
entries.description: Delivering context through action and object, not the tour-guide voice explaining a period to its natives.
entries.principle: The past must be conveyed without stopping the story to explain it, so the craft is to deliver context through action, object and consequence rather than through a narrator or character lecturing the reader. The tour-guide voice, explaining a period to people who live in it, is the genre's most common exposition failure.
entries.example: A scene that lets a custom, a law or a technology reveal itself through what it does to a character teaches the reader more, and more invisibly, than a paragraph explaining it would.
entries.application: Convert exposition into pressure on a character, and never have one period figure explain to another something both would already know for the reader's benefit; if the reader needs it, deliver it through consequence.

entries.name: Forms of Address and Naming
entries.description: Forms of address encode rank, kinship and faith; modern flatness dissolves the social order.
entries.principle: How people addressed one another encodes a period's whole structure of rank, kinship, intimacy and religion, so getting titles, honorifics and names right is not pedantry but the reconstruction of a social order. Modern flatness in address quietly dissolves the hierarchy the period lived by.
entries.example: The difference between a first name, a title and a formula of deference marked relationships a modern reader would otherwise miss, so the forms of address carry information that dialogue content alone cannot.
entries.application: Learn how your period's people named and addressed each other across rank and situation, and let the shifts, the sudden use of a first name, the withheld title, do dramatic work rather than defaulting to modern informality.

entries.name: Keep the Material Constraints Honest
entries.description: Money, distance and time are the period's physics; violate them and the reader stops forgiving.
entries.principle: Money, distance and time are the period's unglamorous physics, and they must stay accurate even when the plot would prefer otherwise, because a reader forgives invented people but not a violated world. What a journey cost, how long it took and what a wage would buy are constraints that generate story when respected.
entries.example: A character crossing a country in implausible time, or affording what their station could not, breaks the material world more damagingly than a factual slip, because it makes the whole reconstruction feel weightless.
entries.application: Fix the real costs, durations and distances of your period and let them constrain the plot, treating the friction they create as a source of drama rather than an obstacle to smooth away.

entries.name: The Known Ending and the Unknown One
entries.description: The reader knows the larger outcome but not this one's; build suspense from the specific and personal.
entries.principle: The historical novel's distinctive structural problem is that the reader often knows the larger story's outcome but not this one's, so suspense must be built from the specific and the personal rather than the general and the famous. The fall of a dynasty is not in doubt; what it costs these characters is.
entries.example: A reader of a Tudor novel knows Anne Boleyn dies, so the tension lives entirely in the texture of how it happens and what it means to the people around it, which is where the book must generate its uncertainty.
entries.application: Locate your suspense in outcomes the reader cannot look up, the fate of your invented figures and the meaning of documented events for them, and narrate the famous outcome as if it were still contingent to those living it.

entries.name: The Real Person as Character
entries.description: A documented real person binds interiority to evidence; the reader can check you, so survive the check.
entries.principle: Putting a documented real person on the page binds interpretation to evidence in a way an invented character escapes, and the craft is to imagine an interior consistent with the record without contradicting the documented life. The reader can check you, and the book's authority depends on surviving the check.
entries.example: A biographical novel that fills a real figure's undocumented thoughts while honouring every known date and act earns its portrait, whereas one that bends the documented life to the plot forfeits the fidelity its form implies.
entries.application: For each real person, separate what the record establishes from what you must imagine, keep your invention consistent with the evidence, and decide how your author's note will signal where interpretation begins.

entries.name: Composite and Compression
entries.description: Composite and compression are legitimate but contradict the record, so must be handled knowingly.
entries.principle: Novels routinely combine several real figures into one, or telescope events that took years into a tighter span, and these are legitimate tools, but they contradict the record and so must be handled knowingly and usually declared. Undeclared compression can quietly assert a false chronology as fact.
entries.example: A single character standing for several historical people, or a decade's events compressed into a season, serves the story while departing from the record, which is why the practised novelist marks such choices rather than presenting them as documentary.
entries.application: Use composites and compression where the story needs them, but track them as departures from the record, and disclose the significant ones so the reader does not carry an invented chronology away as history.

entries.name: Sensory Reconstruction
entries.description: Sensory reconstruction that does dramatic work, not a catalogue standing in for a scene.
entries.principle: The past looked, smelled and sounded unlike the present, and reconstructing its sensory world is part of the claim, but the danger is the catalogue, the inventory of authentic sensations standing in for a scene. Sensory detail earns its place by doing dramatic work, not by proving research.
entries.example: A period rendered through the specific smell, noise and light a character actually registers in a charged moment convinces, while a paragraph itemising every authentic sight and sound reads as a museum label.
entries.application: Choose the few sensory details a character would notice under the pressure of the scene, and let them carry period and emotion together, rather than reconstructing the sensory world exhaustively and calling it immersion.

entries.name: Frame and Vantage
entries.description: Choosing the narrator is choosing which archive the book trusts and which silence it inherits.
entries.principle: Who narrates a historical novel, and from which side of the record, is a claim in itself, because the vantage determines whose account survives to be told. Choosing the narrator is choosing which archive the book trusts and which silence it inherits or contests.
entries.example: A war narrated from the losing side, or a household seen through the servant rather than the master, reconstructs the same events into a different history, so the frame is an argument about the record before a word of plot is written.
entries.application: Choose your narrating vantage deliberately as a claim about whose history you are telling, and test whether the events would look the same from the side whose records did not survive, letting that test shape the frame.

entries.name: The Claim-Type Audit
entries.description: The working method: audit every major scene against the four diagnostic questions.
entries.principle: The diagnostic block resolves into a working method: audit every major scene against the four questions, what claim it makes, where its invention begins, how it handles silence, and what authenticity it owes. A scene that cannot answer probably belongs to a different book, or a different collection.
entries.example: Running a doubtful chapter through the four questions typically reveals which one it is failing, an unearned modern conscience, a hidden contradiction of the record, a silence filled too confidently, or a contract with the reader it has not met.
entries.application: Make the four questions a revision pass, applying them to each significant scene, and treat a scene that answers none of them as a signal to cut, relocate or rebuild it rather than to ship it and hope.

entries.name: The Invented Protagonist Among Real Events
entries.description: The classic engine: an invented protagonist carrying the emotion through documented events.
entries.principle: The classic engine of the historical novel is a fictional protagonist moving through documented events, so the reader meets the great forces of an age through a figure the author is free to invent. The invented centre carries the emotional weight the record cannot supply, while the real events supply the stakes.
entries.example: Walter Scott's Waverley (1814) established the model, sending an ordinary young man through the Jacobite rising so that a national convulsion is felt through one middling, invented life.
entries.application: Build your invented protagonist to be present at the events that matter without altering their documented course, and let their freedom to feel and choose carry the drama the fixed historical outcome cannot.

entries.name: The Real Person in a Supporting Role
entries.description: A real person in a supporting role still owes fidelity; a false cameo is still a false claim.
entries.principle: A documented figure used in a supporting part must be handled with the fidelity their reality demands even when they are not the focus, because a cameo that falsifies a real person is still a false claim. Small roles are where lazy invention most often slips through.
entries.example: A historical monarch, general or writer who crosses a fictional protagonist's path should behave consistently with the record even in a single scene, or the reconstruction pays for the liberty.
entries.application: Give every real person, however minor, the same factual discipline as your leads, and if you cannot make a documented figure serve the scene without distorting them, invent a fictional stand-in instead.

entries.name: Managing the Large Cast
entries.description: The large cast against the reader's memory; names and roles introduced and distinguished with care.
entries.principle: Historical novels tend toward large casts, and the reader's memory is the real constraint, so names, roles and relationships must be introduced and distinguished with care. A reader who loses track of who is who loses the history the cast was meant to convey.
entries.example: A sprawling dynastic or political novel succeeds partly through the craft of making dozens of figures individually memorable, by distinct function, voice or detail, rather than by relying on the reader to hold a genealogy.
entries.application: Introduce your cast at a rate the reader can absorb, differentiate names and voices to reduce confusion, and give each significant figure a clear function, cutting or combining those who exist only to swell the roll.

entries.name: Time Across Decades
entries.description: Moving across decades without going slack; what to dramatise and what to skip is the architecture.
entries.principle: Sagas and multi-generational novels must move across years or lifetimes without going slack, so the architecture of chapters, sections and ellipses becomes a primary craft problem. What to dramatise and what to skip determines whether the sweep reads as consequence or as summary.
entries.example: A family novel that leaps a decade between sections, dramatising only the hinge moments, keeps causality taut where a continuous chronicle would sag under its own duration.
entries.application: Decide which moments across your span must be lived on the page and which can be crossed by ellipsis, and let each dramatised scene be a hinge on which the following years turn rather than an evenly spaced report.

entries.name: Staging the Set-Piece Event
entries.description: Staging the set-piece through the protagonist's partial, embodied experience, not an overhead summary.
entries.principle: A battle, coronation, disaster or trial is a set-piece the historical novel is expected to deliver, and the craft is to stage it through the protagonist's partial, embodied experience rather than as an overhead summary. The famous event must serve the story, not suspend it for a history lesson.
entries.example: A battle seen from one frightened, ill-informed participant conveys both the event and its human meaning, where a narrator's strategic overview would inform the reader while stalling the novel.
entries.application: Anchor every large historical event in a character's limited vantage, delivering the documented shape of the event through what one person can see, do and misunderstand within it.

entries.name: Dramatic Irony From Foreknowledge
entries.description: Foreknowledge as a resource: dramatic irony that deepens pathos without becoming a knowing wink.
entries.principle: The reader's knowledge of how the larger story ends is a resource unique to the genre, generating dramatic irony as characters act in ignorance of an outcome the reader already carries. Used well it deepens pathos; overused it turns the book into a knowing wink.
entries.example: A character laying confident plans the reader knows history will destroy acquires a tragic charge available only because the reader knows more than the character does.
entries.application: Exploit the gap between the reader's foreknowledge and the character's ignorance for irony and pathos, but do not let the narration flaunt its hindsight, keeping the characters fully inside their own uncertain present.

entries.name: The Frame and the Found Manuscript
entries.description: A frame or found manuscript foregrounds constructed knowledge but must earn its distance.
entries.principle: A framing device, a discovered document, a narrator recalling from old age, a modern researcher, can motivate the telling and foreground the constructed nature of historical knowledge, but it also adds distance and risk. The frame must earn its interruption of the past it surrounds.
entries.example: A novel that presents itself as a recovered memoir or a found archive uses the device to raise questions about reliability and transmission, though a frame that merely delays the story pays a price in immediacy.
entries.application: Adopt a frame only where it does thematic work about how the past is known or transmitted, and if it earns its place, integrate it so the reader is never merely waiting to return to the real story inside it.

entries.name: The Translation Convention
entries.description: The translation convention: modern English for a foreign tongue under an unspoken contract.
entries.principle: When characters would have spoken a foreign or archaic tongue, the novel renders it in modern English under an unspoken contract that the reader agrees to accept the rendering as the original. Breaking that contract inconsistently, sprinkling untranslated period words for flavour, can undermine the illusion it means to support.
entries.example: A novel set entirely among speakers of Latin, Mandarin or Old Norse presents their speech in fluent English, and the reader accepts this as translation rather than as the characters speaking English.
entries.application: Establish and keep a consistent convention for representing the characters' actual language, and use untranslated period or foreign terms sparingly and purposefully rather than as decoration that reminds the reader the English is a fiction.

entries.name: Dialect and Accent on the Page
entries.description: Dialect suggested through rhythm, vocabulary and syntax, not reproduced in heavy phonetic spelling.
entries.principle: Regional, class or period speech is best suggested through rhythm, vocabulary and syntax rather than reproduced through heavy phonetic spelling, which slows the reader and can tip into caricature. The goal is the flavour of a voice, not a transcription of it.
entries.example: A few well-chosen words and a distinctive cadence can evoke a dialect far more effectively than pages of respelled phonetics, which exhaust the reader and often patronise the speaker.
entries.application: Convey accent and dialect through diction and rhythm, reserve phonetic spelling for rare emphasis, and check that your rendering of a group's speech does not slide from characterisation into mockery.

entries.name: Religion as Lived Reality
entries.description: Faith rendered as the medium of experience, not quaint colour observed by a secular narrator.
entries.principle: For most of history faith was not a theme but the medium of experience, so a period's cosmology must operate as fact within the book, shaping decisions, fears and hopes. Treating belief as quaint colour observed by a secular narrator falsifies the mentality more than any misplaced object.
entries.example: A medieval novel in which damnation, miracle and the just price are real forces on the characters reconstructs the age's mind, where one in which faith is merely decorative leaves the modern reader outside it.
entries.application: Let your period's religious understanding function as reality within the story, driving choices the characters experience as rational, rather than positioning the narrative to observe their belief from a modern, sceptical distance.

entries.name: Rank and Deference in Scene
entries.description: Rank reconstructed through behaviour and deference; modern egalitarian manners dissolve the hierarchy.
entries.principle: A period's social order lived in the small enactments of rank, address, precedence and deference, so the hierarchy is best reconstructed through behaviour rather than exposition. Modern egalitarian manners quietly dissolve a stratification the period took as the structure of reality.
entries.example: Who sits, who stands, who speaks first and who is addressed by title enacts a social order in a single scene more completely than a paragraph explaining the class system could.
entries.application: Stage your period's hierarchy through the physical and verbal behaviour it demanded, and let violations of that order, a withheld bow, a presumptuous familiarity, carry the dramatic charge they would really have held.

entries.name: Depicting Period Violence
entries.description: Period violence rendered without flinching into vagueness or lingering into spectacle.
entries.principle: Historical violence must be rendered with accuracy that neither flinches into vagueness nor lingers into spectacle, because both evasions betray the reality. The craft is to convey what violence meant and cost in its period without either sanitising it or serving it up as entertainment.
entries.example: A rendering that conveys the specific brutality of a period's warfare or punishment, and its meaning to those who witnessed it, teaches more than either a discreet cutaway or a dwelt-upon gore scene.
entries.application: Show your period's violence at the level of accuracy the subject requires, calibrated to the claim the book is making, and avoid both the euphemism that denies it and the relish that exploits it.

entries.name: Intimacy and Sex in Period
entries.description: Intimacy reconstructed with period attitudes; importing modern norms of consent and identity is presentism.
entries.principle: Sexual and romantic life must be reconstructed with period attitudes rather than modern ones, since expectations, constraints, dangers and meanings differed profoundly. Importing contemporary norms of consent, desire and identity into the past is a form of presentism that can distort the very stakes of a scene.
entries.example: A relationship governed by a period's real constraints on women's agency, on marriage, on the consequences of transgression, carries dramatic weight that a modern sensibility grafted onto the characters would erase.
entries.application: Reconstruct intimacy through your period's actual attitudes and dangers, and where those attitudes are troubling, render them honestly rather than modernising them, letting the historical constraint generate the scene's real tension.

entries.name: The Agrarian Year
entries.description: The agrarian year as determinant, not backdrop: what characters could do, eat, travel and survive.
entries.principle: Before industrialisation the calendar of weather, harvest, daylight and season governed nearly everything, so a pre-modern world that ignores the agrarian year rings false. Season is not backdrop but a determinant of what characters could do, eat, travel and survive.
entries.example: A rural pre-modern novel in which planting, harvest, winter scarcity and the length of the working day shape the plot reconstructs a rhythm of life the modern reader no longer feels but the period lived by.
entries.application: Anchor your pre-modern story in the real cycle of season and harvest, letting the calendar constrain travel, food, labour and mood, so the natural year presses on the characters as it pressed on their originals.

entries.name: The Place as Character
entries.description: A vanished built environment made a protagonist, rebuilt from evidence rather than imagined generically.
entries.principle: Reconstructing a vanished built environment, a city, a house, a landscape as it then was, can give a novel a protagonist that outlives its people. The place must be rebuilt from evidence rather than imagined generically, and then made to shape the lives within it.
entries.example: A novel that reconstructs a specific historical city so thoroughly that its streets, trades and quarters determine what happens there turns the setting into an agent rather than a stage.
entries.application: Research your setting as it actually was at your chosen moment, then let its real geography, architecture and economy constrain and generate the action, so the place is reconstructed rather than furnished.

entries.name: Work and Process
entries.description: Work and process: how things were made, a rich and least-clichéd source of period reality.
entries.principle: How things were actually made, grown, built and done is one of the richest and least clichéd sources of period reality, because labour and craft were most people's daily experience. Rendering a real process with understanding conveys a period more convincingly than its costumes or banquets.
entries.example: A scene that shows the genuine steps and skills of a period trade, the forge, the loom, the sail, the scriptorium, carries authority precisely because the process is real and specific.
entries.application: Learn a relevant period process well enough to dramatise its real steps and difficulties, and let the labour of your characters, rendered accurately, do the immersive work that ornament cannot.

entries.name: The Limited Narrator
entries.description: A limited narrator turns the exposition problem into a source of tension.
entries.principle: A child, an outsider or an otherwise restricted narrator can manage exposition and irony at once, because their partial understanding lets the reader see more than the narrator does. Limited knowledge turns the exposition problem into a source of tension.
entries.example: A young or naive narrator who reports a period accurately while misreading it allows the reader to grasp what the narrator cannot, delivering context through dramatic irony rather than explanation.
entries.application: Consider a narrator whose limited grasp of their world lets you show the period through their misunderstandings, using the gap between what they report and what the reader infers to carry both information and irony.

entries.name: The Documentary Interleave
entries.description: Interleaved documents deepen the reconstruction, but each must earn its place and match its period.
entries.principle: Braiding real or invented documents into the narrative, epigraphs, letters, reports, records, can deepen the reconstruction and foreground how the past is known, but each interleaved document must earn its place and match its period. A misjudged or anachronistic insert damages more than plain prose would.
entries.example: A novel that opens chapters with period documents, or threads letters and reports through the story, can make the archive itself part of the reading experience when the inserts are authentic in form and function.
entries.application: Interleave documents only where they add something narration cannot, ensure each matches the form and voice of its period, and if you invent a document, give it the shape a real one of that kind would have had.

entries.name: The Aftermath Problem
entries.description: When the climax is fixed and famous, meaning is found in the aftermath; the close is elegiac.
entries.principle: Because the documented climax of a historical story is often fixed and famous, the ending must find meaning in the aftermath, in what the known outcome costs and leaves, rather than in surprise. The genre's characteristic close is elegiac, settling accounts the history has already decided.
entries.example: A novel whose central event the reader knows in advance earns its ending by dramatising the consequences for its people, the grief, the survival, the changed world, rather than by withholding an outcome that was never in doubt.
entries.application: Plan your ending around the meaning and cost of the known outcome rather than its revelation, and let the final movement account for what the documented event did to the invented lives that carried the reader through it.

entries.name: Standalone or Saga
entries.description: Standalone or saga: a scope choice that makes different promises and demands different architecture.
entries.principle: Scope is an early and consequential craft decision: a single self-contained novel and a multi-volume saga make different promises and demand different architectures. Choosing the wrong scale for the material strands a saga's sweep in one book or stretches a single story thin across many.
entries.example: A tightly focused historical event may want one disciplined volume, while the rise of a family or a nation may require the room only a series provides, and the material usually indicates which.
entries.application: Match your scope to the story's real span before drafting, and if the material is a single arc, resist inflating it, while if it is generational, plan the architecture a longer form requires from the start.

entries.name: The Multi-Volume Historical
entries.description: The multi-volume historical must sustain momentum and memory across books, each with its own shape.
entries.principle: A series spanning a life, a war or a nation must sustain momentum and memory across books, giving each volume its own shape while advancing the whole. The risk is a middle volume that marks time, or a reader who cannot re-enter the world after a gap.
entries.example: A long historical sequence succeeds by making each book satisfying in itself while the larger arc accumulates, rather than treating early volumes as mere setup for a distant payoff.
entries.application: Give every volume a complete internal movement even as it serves the larger sweep, and build in the reminders and re-entries a reader returning after a year will need, so no book is only a bridge.

entries.name: The Archive as a Writer's Tool
entries.description: The novelist mines the archive for concrete, strange, human detail, not for an argument.
entries.principle: The novelist uses primary sources differently from the scholar, mining them for the concrete, the strange and the human detail that ignites a scene rather than for an argument. The archive's value to fiction is the specific texture the secondary summary strips out.
entries.example: A single vivid particular from a letter, an inventory or a court record, an object, a phrase, a sum of money, can seed a scene in a way no general history could, because it carries the grain of the real.
entries.application: Read primary sources for the specific detail that sparks imagination, collecting the concrete and the odd rather than the summarisable, and let those particulars anchor invented scenes in real texture.

entries.name: Reading Against the Grain to Generate Scenes
entries.description: Reading a hostile source against its purpose to generate scenes from what it tried to suppress.
entries.principle: A hostile or self-interested source can be read against its purpose to generate fiction, since what a document tried to suppress or reduce often points to the story worth telling. The runaway ad, the indictment, the tax record can each be turned into a life.
entries.example: A person reduced to a description in a document made to control them can become a protagonist when the novelist reads that document for the life it was trying to erase.
entries.application: Take your period's controlling documents and read them for the people they were built to flatten, letting the gap between the record's purpose and its subject's humanity become the space your fiction fills.

entries.name: The Expert and the Sensitivity Reader
entries.description: Expert and sensitivity readers catch errors of fact and framing a reference-grade book can't afford.
entries.principle: A reconstruction benefits from readers who know the period, the place or the community better than the author, catching errors of fact and of framing before publication. Declining that check, especially on sensitive material, ships avoidable failures a reference-grade book cannot afford.
entries.example: An expert reader can catch an anachronism or a misused source, and a reader from a depicted community can flag a framing that the author could not see, each strengthening the book's authority.
entries.application: Seek out readers with knowledge you lack, of the period's detail and of any living community you depict, and treat their corrections as improvements to the claim your book is making rather than as concessions.

entries.name: The Anachronism Pass
entries.description: The anachronism pass: a dedicated revision stage hunting period-misfit objects, words and assumptions.
entries.principle: Anachronism is best hunted in a dedicated revision pass rather than caught by chance during drafting, because factual and mental anachronisms hide in the ordinary. A pass that interrogates objects, words and assumptions for their period fit is a distinct editorial stage.
entries.example: A revision that checks each named object and term against its real date, and each attitude against its period plausibility, catches what continuous drafting attention misses because the errors feel natural.
entries.application: Run a deliberate anachronism pass late in revision, checking vocabulary, objects, institutions and, hardest of all, the characters' assumptions, treating anything you cannot date or justify as suspect until confirmed.

entries.name: The Author's Note as Craft
entries.description: The author's note as composed craft, deciding which departures to disclose as a contract with the reader.
entries.principle: The author's note is a composed part of the book, not a disclaimer, and its craft is deciding what to disclose, the departures, compressions and inventions, and how to frame the contract with the reader. A well-made note strengthens the reconstruction by showing its seams honestly.
entries.example: A note that names which characters and events are documented, where the author departed from the record and why, lets the reader trust the rest and understand the kind of claim the book has made.
entries.application: Write your note as carefully as your chapters, disclosing the significant departures from the record and the reasoning behind them, so the reader closes the book knowing exactly where fact ended and invention began.

entries.name: Point of View and the Historical Narrator
entries.description: The tension between a period-limited point of view and a modern narrating intelligence.
entries.principle: Historical fiction lives in a tension between a period-limited point of view, which knows only what a character could know, and a modern narrating intelligence, which can supply context and irony. Managing that tension, deciding how much the narration knows beyond the characters, is a defining craft choice.
entries.example: A close point of view confined to a character's period knowledge maximises immersion, while a more knowing narrator can frame and interpret, and many historical novels negotiate a deliberate position between the two.
entries.application: Decide consciously how far your narration exceeds your characters' knowledge, keep that distance consistent, and let it serve the book's claim, choosing immersion or interpretation rather than drifting between them by accident.

entries.name: Foreshadowing a Documented Outcome
entries.description: Foreshadowing a known outcome by deepening dread, not by hinting at a surprise there is none of.
entries.principle: When the outcome is known to the reader, foreshadowing must work by deepening dread and meaning rather than by hinting at a surprise there is none of. The craft is to make the inevitable feel weighted rather than to pretend it is uncertain.
entries.example: A narrative that lets the reader feel a documented catastrophe gathering, without insulting their foreknowledge by feigning suspense about whether it will come, converts inevitability into tragic momentum.
entries.application: Foreshadow known outcomes to intensify their weight, not to manufacture false uncertainty, and trust the reader's knowledge of what is coming to do work that a concealed twist could not.

entries.name: The Counterfactual Pressure Within History
entries.description: Generating tension from felt contingency, a hinge that might have turned, without leaving the record.
entries.principle: A realist historical novel can generate tension by making the reader feel that events might have gone otherwise, without leaving the documented record. The sense of contingency, of a hinge that could have turned differently, is available even when the outcome is fixed.
entries.example: A novel that dramatises the real alternatives its characters believed they faced makes a settled history feel contingent again, restoring the openness the participants experienced.
entries.application: Recover the genuine uncertainty your historical figures lived inside, dramatising the paths that seemed open to them, so the reader feels the contingency of an outcome the record has already closed.

entries.name: The Object as Anchor
entries.description: A single artefact carried through the book concentrates a period and binds its scenes.
entries.principle: A single artefact carried through a novel can concentrate a period and bind its scenes, giving the reader a material anchor for an unfamiliar world. The object works when it is real to its period and made to accumulate meaning, not when it is a mere prop.
entries.example: A book, a coin, a garment or a tool that passes through a story can carry the history it witnesses, becoming a thread of continuity and a focus for the period's meaning.
entries.application: Consider anchoring your novel in a period-accurate object that recurs and gathers significance, letting it localise the reader in the world and carry theme through its passage across the story.

entries.name: The Invented Setting in a Real Matrix
entries.description: An invented setting inside a real matrix: freedom that must stay plausible and never contradict its history.
entries.principle: Placing an invented town, house or family within a real historical matrix gives the novelist freedom while preserving authenticity, since the fictional locus can be shaped to the story while the surrounding history stays fixed. The invented setting must be plausible for its real context and must not contradict it.
entries.example: A fictional village set precisely within a documented region and period lets the author control the stage while the real economy, politics and events of the surrounding world press on it accurately.
entries.application: Invent the specific locus your plot needs, then embed it rigorously in the real geography, economy and history around it, so the freedom of the fictional place never violates the documented world it sits inside.

entries.name: Rendering a Mentality
entries.description: Rendering a mentality so an alien value system feels like reason to those who hold it.
entries.principle: The deepest reconstruction is of a mentality, a period's structure of belief, honour, fate or obligation that a modern reader does not share, and rendering it from the inside is the genre's most demanding task. The aim is to make an alien value system feel like reason to those who hold it.
entries.example: A novel that makes a period's sense of honour, damnation or duty operate as compelling logic within its characters achieves an immersion that accurate objects and settings alone cannot reach.
entries.application: Identify the governing values your period held that a modern reader would not, and dramatise characters acting on them as self-evident, so the reader comes to feel the internal coherence of a worldview they do not share.

entries.name: Sympathy for an Accurate Cast
entries.description: Managing sympathy for an accurate cast without granting them an anachronistic conscience.
entries.principle: When period accuracy produces characters whose values are hard for a modern reader to like, the craft is to manage sympathy without falsifying them, granting complexity and understanding rather than an anachronistic conscience. The reader can be brought to comprehend a character they would never endorse.
entries.example: A protagonist whose real period views are troubling can hold a reader through depth, consistency and human contradiction, where a version softened into modern acceptability would be both duller and less true.
entries.application: Earn the reader's engagement with a difficult but accurate character through interiority and complexity rather than through moral anachronism, letting comprehension rather than approval carry the relationship.

entries.name: Pacing the Research Reveal
entries.description: Pacing the research reveal between overwhelming exposition and an under-realised world.
entries.principle: A richly researched world must be revealed at a rate the reader can absorb, dosed so the period unfolds without either overwhelming exposition or a thin, under-realised setting. Pacing the reveal is the difference between immersion and either a lecture or a void.
entries.example: A novel that releases its world detail steadily, tied to what each scene needs, builds a dense period without stalling, where front-loaded research or withheld context each break the immersion differently.
entries.application: Meter your world's detail to the reader's absorption, introducing what each scene requires when it requires it, and resist both the urge to explain everything early and the neglect that leaves the period unfurnished.

entries.name: Terrain and Climate as Constraint
entries.description: Terrain and climate press on the plot through the society that meets them, without lapsing into determinism.
entries.principle: Landscape, weather and environment are constraints on historical action as much as on modern, shaping travel, warfare, agriculture and survival, but they act through the society that meets them rather than as simple causes. The craft is to let terrain and climate press on the plot without lapsing into determinism.
entries.example: A campaign undone by mud and winter, or a settlement shaped by a river and a growing season, reconstructs the real weight of environment on human action while keeping the outcome a matter of how people responded.
entries.application: Let your period's terrain and climate genuinely constrain what characters can do, routing their effects through the society's real capacities, and avoid both a weightless world and a crude weather-as-cause story.

entries.name: The Sensitive-Material Craft Screen
entries.description: The sensitive-material screen: named plainly, run through the four questions, as routine craft.
entries.principle: Where a book carries slavery, colonialism, genocide or occupation, the sensitive material is handled as craft: named plainly in the scene's own terms, then treated with the four diagnostic questions, neither censored nor relished. The heightened stakes of this genre make the screen a routine part of composition, not a special apparatus.
entries.example: A scene depicting an atrocity that states what it is plainly and then answers for the claim it makes teaches method, while one that either averts its eyes or lingers for effect fails the material in opposite directions.
entries.application: Run any scene of historical atrocity or oppression through the diagnostic questions and the plain-naming rule, deciding what claim it makes about real people whose descendants are alive, and build it to answer for that claim as a normal part of the drafting.

entries.name: The Claim-Type Audit
entries.description: Run before drafting and again in revision. Any single "no" is a stop, not a note. Establishes what kind of claim about the past the book is making before and after a scene is written.
items: Can you state in one sentence what kind of claim this book makes about the past: fidelity, recovery, emotional truth, or deliberate invention against the record?
For each major scene, can you point to where the documented record ends and your invention begins?
Have you decided, for each silence the book crosses, whether it is filled, marked as a gap, or held by a community elsewhere?
Does the level of authenticity you are supplying match what this particular book's reader actually requires?
Does every scene trace back to one of these four questions, and have you relocated or cut those that answer none?

entries.name: The Anachronism Screen
entries.description: A dedicated late-revision pass. Factual and mental anachronisms hide in the ordinary and must be hunted deliberately, not caught by chance.
items: Has every named object, food, material and technology been checked against its real date of availability in this place?
Has every distinctive word and idiom been checked for a coinage date later than the scene?
Do the institutions, laws and offices referenced actually exist in this period under these names?
Do the characters hold assumptions plausible for their time rather than a modern conscience?
Have units of money, distance and time been kept consistent with the period rather than modern equivalents?

entries.name: Writing Across Identity and Culture
entries.description: Apply whenever the book depicts a people, culture or community not the author's own. Stakes are heightened in this genre because the depicted are often the historically silenced.
items: Have you researched the depicted culture from its own sources and scholarship, not only from outsiders' accounts?
Are you reproducing the colonizer's or dominant group's categories, or writing against them?
Where the culture is living, have you distinguished a dead archive from a tradition held by present custodians?
Have you sought a reader from or expert in the depicted community before publication?
Does the depiction leave the reader better informed about why the standard genre treatment fails, rather than better equipped to repeat it?

entries.name: Depicting Atrocity
entries.description: Apply to any scene depicting slavery, genocide, colonial violence, occupation or mass suffering. Named plainly, analysed as craft, neither censored nor relished.
items: Is the atrocity named plainly in the scene's own terms rather than euphemised or aestheticised?
What kind of claim is the book making about the real people this happened to, and can it answer for that claim?
Are the descendants of the victims alive, and does that change what the book owes?
Does the scene carry both the documented failures and any legitimate artistic use, rather than teaching avoidance?
Is the suffering doing craft work, or is it a backdrop for a character's growth or the reader's comfort?

entries.name: The Source Reliability Screen
entries.description: Apply to every load-bearing fact. Consensus among secondary sources is not independent confirmation when they copy one another.
items: Have you traced the fact to the primary artefact rather than a citation of it?
How many layers of transcription, translation, editing and summary stand between you and the original?
If every source traces to one intermediary, are you treating the fact as single-sourced?
What was the original document made for, and in which direction does that purpose bias it?
Have you dated your secondary sources and checked whether their consensus has since been overturned?

entries.name: The Real Person Screen
entries.description: Apply to every documented real person on the page, major or minor. The reader can check you, and a cameo that falsifies a real person is still a false claim.
items: Have you separated what the record establishes about this person from what you must imagine?
Does your invention stay consistent with the documented dates, acts and whereabouts?
Where you contradict the record rather than fill a gap, is the contradiction deliberate and declared?
For a recently living person, have you considered the difference between a documented fact and an unsupported allegation?
Will your author's note signal where interpretation of this person begins?

entries.name: The Living Tradition Screen
entries.description: Apply before using any past held by a present community: oral history, sacred narrative, or a still-mourned recent event. "There is no record" is often false.
items: Is the past you are using held by a living community rather than an ownerless archive?
Does the tradition carry rules about who may tell it and to whom?
Have you researched it with its custodians, or are you extracting it from a distance?
Where you may not use it, have you found a way to write around it rather than through it?
Are you treating a living inheritance as raw material, and if so, is that defensible?

entries.name: The Presentism Screen
entries.description: Apply to characters' values, not just their facts. Presentism falsifies the past more deeply than any misplaced object.
items: Do your period characters hold assumptions their time actually held, however uncomfortable?
Have you avoided giving a sympathetic character an implausibly modern conscience?
Where a protagonist's real views are repellent, are they rendered truthfully rather than cleaned up?
Does the book's judgement live in its structure rather than in anachronistic dissent voiced by characters?
Have you checked that the reader is not being flattered by a past conveniently agreeing with the present?

entries.name: The Dialogue Register Screen
entries.description: Apply to all period speech. Avoid both the mock-antique that no one spoke and the modern idiom that drops the reader out.
items: Is the register a plausible plainness rather than forsooth-and-prithee pastiche?
Have individual words and idioms been checked for anachronistic coinage?
Is dialect suggested through rhythm and diction rather than heavy phonetic spelling?
Does your rendering of a group's speech characterise rather than caricature?
Is your convention for representing a foreign or period language consistent throughout?

entries.name: The Information-Flow Screen
entries.description: Apply to every plot point that depends on a character knowing something. Information moved at the speed of its period.
items: Could this character actually know this, by this point, given how news travelled?
Have you mapped the real speed of letters, riders, ships and rumour in this period?
Do delays, gaps and unreliability in transmission generate the plot rather than being overridden?
Are maps, records and reference works available to the character only where they would really exist?
Does any character act on intelligence that could not yet have reached them?

entries.name: The Material-Constraint Screen
entries.description: Apply to journeys, purchases and durations. A reader forgives invented people but not a violated world.
items: Does each journey take a period-plausible time given the real means of travel?
Can each character afford what they buy or do, given their real station and its income?
Are durations, seasons and daylight consistent with the period's actual conditions?
Do the material costs and frictions of the world generate drama rather than being smoothed away?
Have you resisted letting the plot quietly grant modern speed, wealth or convenience?

entries.name: The Sensory-Detail Screen
entries.description: Apply to descriptive passages. Sensory detail earns its place by doing work, not by proving research.
items: Does each sensory detail belong to what a character would actually notice under this scene's pressure?
Have you cut the inventory of authentic sensations that stands in for a scene?
Do the chosen details carry period and emotion together rather than either alone?
Is the sensory world specific to this exact place and moment rather than generically old?
Would removing a detail cost the scene anything beyond a display of research?

entries.name: The Author's Note Screen
entries.description: Apply when composing the note. The note is a contract with the reader about the boundary between the found and the made.
items: Does the note state which characters and events are documented?
Does it disclose the significant departures from the record and the reasoning behind them?
Are compressions and composites of real people or events acknowledged?
Does it credit the research base without implying the invention is itself research?
Would a reader close the book knowing where fact ended and invention began?

entries.name: The Composite and Compression Screen
entries.description: Apply wherever real figures are combined or real timelines are tightened. These contradict the record and must be handled knowingly.
items: Have you tracked every place where several real people are combined into one character?
Have you tracked every place where events spanning years are compressed into a shorter span?
Are these departures deliberate choices serving the story rather than accidents?
Will the significant ones be disclosed so the reader does not carry an invented chronology away as fact?
Does any compression assert a false causal sequence the reader might take as documented?

entries.name: The Intimacy and Consent-History Screen
entries.description: Apply to romantic and sexual content. Reconstruct period attitudes rather than importing modern ones; render troubling norms honestly rather than modernising them.
items: Are the constraints, dangers and meanings of intimacy specific to this period rather than contemporary?
Where period norms of consent and agency are troubling, are they rendered truthfully rather than sanitised?
Does the historical constraint generate the scene's real tension rather than being overridden?
Are you distinguishing depicting a period attitude from endorsing it?
Does the material's handling match the claim the book is making about the past?

entries.name: The Publication-Readiness Screen
entries.description: Run last, before the manuscript is final. The reference-grade reconstruction cannot afford avoidable failures.
items: Has a dedicated anachronism pass been completed on words, objects, institutions and attitudes?
Has an expert reader in the period or place reviewed the manuscript?
Where a living community is depicted, has a reader from it been consulted?
Is every cited real work, document and person a published or documented one a reader could verify?
Have the four diagnostic questions been applied to every scene of sensitive material?

entries.name: Scott and the Invention of the Form
entries.description: Scott fused antiquarian research with the novel, rendering the past as a society with its own logic.
entries.principle: The historical novel as a distinct form is conventionally dated to Walter Scott, who fused antiquarian research with the novel to render the past as a different society with its own logic rather than a costume backdrop. His innovation was the ordinary protagonist through whom vast historical forces are felt.
entries.example: Scott's Waverley (1814), subtitled with a note that its story is set sixty years since, sends a middling young man through the Jacobite rising so a national convulsion arrives as personal experience.
entries.application: Recognise that the genre's founding move, the invented average figure inside real events, is still its central engine, and know what you are inheriting or departing from when you place a fictional protagonist among documented history.

entries.name: Before Scott
entries.description: Before Scott, romance and the Gothic used history as backdrop; his addition was historical causation.
entries.principle: Scott did not invent historical settings, only the form that took the past seriously as a distinct society; before him, romance, antiquarianism and the Gothic used history as backdrop or scenery. Understanding the antecedents clarifies what Scott actually added, which was historical causation.
entries.example: The Gothic novels of the later eighteenth century, with their medieval castles and vague pasts, used history for atmosphere rather than for the reconstruction of a working social order that Scott introduced.
entries.application: Distinguish using the past as atmosphere from reconstructing it as a society, and decide which your book is doing, since the genre's seriousness begins exactly where the past stops being mere scenery.

entries.name: Manzoni and the European Spread
entries.description: Manzoni carried the form into Italy, marrying Scott's method to a moral and linguistic project.
entries.principle: The form crossed quickly into Europe and took national roots, and in Italy Alessandro Manzoni produced a founding novel that married Scott's method to a moral and linguistic project. The historical novel became a vehicle for national self-understanding beyond Britain.
entries.example: Manzoni's The Betrothed (I Promessi Sposi, first published 1827) set its story in seventeenth-century plague Milan and became foundational for the Italian novel and language alike.
entries.application: Study how the form adapted to different national traditions and projects, and recognise that the historical novel has always carried a culture's argument with its own past, not only Britain's.

entries.name: The National-Romance Mode
entries.description: The nineteenth century's dominant mode: national romance, the past as a people's heroic becoming.
entries.principle: Through the nineteenth century the dominant mode was national romance, the past rendered as the heroic becoming of a people, often in service of a rising national consciousness. It is the mode against which the twentieth century would later react.
entries.example: James Fenimore Cooper in America and Victor Hugo in France used the historical novel to narrate national identity, dramatising the past as the story of how the nation came to be itself.
entries.application: Notice when your material tempts you toward national romance, the past as flattering origin story, and decide consciously whether you are examining a founding myth or retelling it in its own terms.
