entries.name: Dumas and the Popular Branch
entries.description: Dumas and the popular branch: the past as adventure, a different claim rather than a lesser one.
entries.principle: Alongside the literary line ran a popular one, serialised and propulsive, that claimed the past as adventure rather than reconstruction. This branch is a large share of what readers have always bought as historical fiction and is not a lesser thing but a different claim.
entries.example: Alexandre Dumas, working in the serial feuilleton, made the seventeenth century a playground in The Three Musketeers (1844), subordinating documentary fidelity to honour and momentum.
entries.application: Locate your book on the spectrum from reconstruction to adventure, and if you are writing in the popular tradition, own it and keep its hard constraints honest rather than apologising for not being the literary kind.

entries.name: Tolstoy and the Boundary
entries.description: Tolstoy as the form's summit and boundary case, drawn from living memory rather than an archive.
entries.principle: The nineteenth century's summit of the form is also its great boundary case, a novel of the recent past drawn from living and family memory rather than reconstructed from an archive. It marks where the genre's definition strains, since its author did not have to rebuild the world he described.
entries.example: Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace (1865 to 1869) narrates the Napoleonic invasion of roughly half a century earlier, drawn from family recollection and oral memory, so it reads as historical fiction while sitting outside a strict author-side definition of it.
entries.application: Use this case to test your own project: ask whether your setting is one you reconstructed or one you or your informants remembered, since the difference determines what kind of historical claim your book can honestly make.

entries.name: Flaubert and the Archaeological Reconstruction
entries.description: Flaubert and total archaeological reconstruction, with its besetting risk of the catalogue.
entries.principle: A distinct strand pursued the total reconstruction of a remote and alien world, valuing immersion and the exotic over the familiar national past. It established the pure-reconstruction ambition and its besetting risk, the catalogue that overwhelms the story.
entries.example: Gustave Flaubert's Salammbô (1862) reconstructed third-century-BC Carthage in dense sensory detail, pursuing an archaeological completeness that dazzled and, to some critics, buried the narrative.
entries.application: When your ambition is total immersion in a remote world, learn from this strand's achievement and its danger, and keep the reconstruction subordinate to a story rather than letting accuracy become the point.

entries.name: The Historical Novel as Nation-Building
entries.description: The historical novel as nation-building, the national-romance mode at its most propagandistic.
entries.principle: In several nations the historical novel served an explicit project of building or sustaining national identity, sometimes under foreign rule, making the form a political instrument. This is the national-romance mode at its most consequential and most propagandistic.
entries.example: Henryk Sienkiewicz wrote his seventeenth-century Trilogy, beginning with With Fire and Sword (1884), avowedly to hearten a partitioned Poland, and received the Nobel Prize in 1905.
entries.application: Recognise the real power of the historical novel to shape a nation's self-image, and take responsibility for whether your book strengthens a myth or interrogates it, since the form has demonstrably done both.

entries.name: The Antiquarian Decline
entries.description: The antiquarian decline: period detail detached from the historical necessity Scott dramatised.
entries.principle: By the later nineteenth century critics saw the form declining into antiquarianism, the accumulation of period detail detached from the historical necessity Scott's best work had dramatised. The decorative historical novel is the failure mode the genre's theory would later diagnose.
entries.example: A wave of costume romances substituted researched surface for the deeper reconstruction of social forces, producing the "decorative" historical novel later theory would contrast with the classical achievement.
entries.application: Guard against the antiquarian trap in your own work, where accurate detail masks the absence of dramatised historical causation, and ask whether your period does anything beyond furnishing the scene.

entries.name: Lukács and the Theory of the Form
entries.description: Lukács's theory: historical necessity portrayed through typical, deliberately average characters.
entries.principle: The foundational theory of the historical novel holds that its achievement is portraying historical necessity through typical, deliberately average characters, so a reader experiences broad social forces through a representative figure while the world-historical individual stays at the margins. It remains the reference point every later theory argues with.
entries.example: Georg Lukács's The Historical Novel, written in the 1930s and published in English translation in 1962, reads Scott, Manzoni and Tolstoy as classical practitioners and ties the form's rise to a post-revolutionary consciousness of history as something that happens to ordinary people.
entries.application: Know the theory your genre argues over: decide whether your protagonist is the Lukácsian typical figure carrying historical forces, or something the theory did not anticipate, and understand the tradition either choice engages.

entries.name: The Early-Twentieth-Century Revival
entries.description: The early-twentieth-century revival interiorised the past, often through a real figure's voice.
entries.principle: The form was renewed in the twentieth century by novels that interiorised the past, often through a real historical figure's first-person voice, restoring psychological depth to reconstruction. This revival established the modern literary historical novel.
entries.example: Robert Graves's I, Claudius (1934) and Marguerite Yourcenar's Memoirs of Hadrian (1951) rebuilt the ancient world from inside a documented consciousness, making interiority the vehicle of historical reconstruction.
entries.application: Study how these novels carried heavy research through deep first-person interiority, and consider the first-person reconstruction of a documented mind as a method for making the remote past intimate.

entries.name: The Serious Classical Novel
entries.description: A revival strand reconstructing classical antiquity's alien mind with scholarship, not exotic backdrop.
entries.principle: A strand of the twentieth-century revival specialised in the rigorous reconstruction of classical antiquity, treating a genuinely alien mentality with scholarship and imaginative seriousness rather than as exotic backdrop. It raised the standard for how far a modern reader could be taken into an ancient mind.
entries.example: Mary Renault's novels of ancient Greece, such as The Last of the Wine (1956) and The King Must Die (1958), reconstructed classical belief, sexuality and politics from inside their own logic.
entries.application: When reconstructing antiquity, aim for the mentality rather than the surface, and learn from this strand that the ancient world convinces most when its alien values are made to operate as reason rather than displayed as strangeness.

entries.name: The Mid-Century Blockbuster
entries.description: The mid-century blockbuster: the researched doorstop reconstructing an era for a mass readership.
entries.principle: The mid twentieth century produced the popular epic historical, the researched doorstop that reconstructs a place or era at length for a mass readership. It is a major part of the genre's real market and established the sweeping, immersive popular mode.
entries.example: James Michener's long place-centred epics, such as Hawaii (1959), reconstructed a whole region's history across generations for a vast audience, defining the popular historical blockbuster.
entries.application: Recognise the blockbuster as a legitimate mode with its own craft of sweep and accessibility, and if you write in it, master the management of scale and the delivery of research to a general reader rather than dismissing the form.

entries.name: The Biographical Novel Emerges
entries.description: The biographical novel emerges as a mode, with its craft problem of fidelity and interpolation.
entries.principle: The twentieth century established fictional biography of real people as a recognisable mode, with its own craft problem of fidelity and interpolation. Whether it is a distinct form or a marketing category remains contested, but its practice became a tradition.
entries.example: Irving Stone popularised the biographical novel with Lust for Life (1934) on Van Gogh and The Agony and the Ecstasy (1961) on Michelangelo, treating the documented life as a discipline with rules of its own.
entries.application: If you fictionalise a real life, join a tradition with established problems, the seam between record and invention, the ethics of imagining a real interior, and study how its practitioners have handled them.

entries.name: Microhistory Crosses Into Fiction
entries.description: Microhistory crosses into fiction, licensing novels centred on the obscure rather than the great.
entries.principle: From the 1970s the historical discipline's turn to microhistory, reconstructing an ordinary life from the records that happened to preserve it, reshaped what the novel could attempt, licensing fiction centred on the obscure rather than the great. The scholarly recovery of the small life fed the fictional one.
entries.example: Works such as Carlo Ginzburg's The Cheese and the Worms (1976) and Natalie Zemon Davis's The Return of Martin Guerre (1983) showed that an ordinary person's world could be reconstructed and openly reasoned about, a method fiction absorbed.
entries.application: Take from microhistory both its subject, the recoverable obscure life, and its discipline, the open marking of where evidence ends, and let the ordinary rather than the famous be your legitimate centre.

entries.name: The Postmodern Turn
entries.description: The postmodern turn: metafiction questioning how the past is known and narrated.
entries.principle: In the later twentieth century the form turned self-conscious, using metafiction and a visible modern perspective to question how the past is known and narrated. The reconstruction became doubled, a claim about the past and about our reading of it.
entries.example: John Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman (1969) narrates a Victorian story through an intrusive modern voice that offers alternative endings, making the constructed nature of historical fiction its subject.
entries.application: Decide whether your book trusts its reconstruction or interrogates it, and if you adopt metafictional or knowing devices, ensure they argue about how this history is known rather than merely signalling cleverness.

entries.name: The Latin American New Historical Novel
entries.description: The Latin American new historical novel made the archive's unreliability a formal principle.
entries.principle: A powerful strand distrusted the official record as method, using deliberate anachronism and the marvellous to contest the histories that colonial and national power had written. It made the unreliability of the archive a formal principle rather than a problem to be hidden.
entries.example: Alejo Carpentier's The Kingdom of This World (1949) and later novels by Fuentes and García Márquez treated the region's suppressed histories as requiring a form that broke with the realist grammar of the official account.
entries.application: Where your subject is a history written by the powerful, consider whether realist fidelity serves it or whether, as this tradition argued, the form itself must contest the record it inherits.

entries.name: Writing Back to Empire
entries.description: Writing back to empire, reconstructing colonised worlds from inside their own logic.
entries.principle: The postcolonial historical novel set out to contest the colonizer's record and to reconstruct pre-colonial and colonised worlds from inside their own logic. It refused the frame the archive imposed and made the recovery of the silenced a central project of the form.
entries.example: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) rebuilt an Igbo society at the moment of colonial contact to answer the European account by declining its vantage, and later writers extended the project across the colonised world.
entries.application: When you work with colonial history, interrogate the provenance of your sources and decide whose frame you are adopting, and learn from this tradition how to reconstruct a world the archive was built to misrepresent.

entries.name: The Recovered Voice
entries.description: The recovered voice: fiction centring the archive's silence about slavery and the unrecorded life.
entries.principle: The late twentieth century's most consequential development was fiction that centred the archive's silence about slavery and made the unrecorded life its subject, doing on the page what theory would later name. It shifted the genre's centre from the powerful to the erased.
entries.example: Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987) reconstructed the interior life of the enslaved from testimony and haunting rather than from a record that never kept it, becoming the paradigm of the recovered-voice historical novel.
entries.application: Recognise that centring the silenced is now a central, not marginal, project of the genre, and if you attempt it, study how its landmark works made absence itself into presence without false documentary confidence.

entries.name: The Theory Catches Up
entries.description: Theory followed the art, naming the practice of narrating around an archival silence.
entries.principle: The critical vocabulary for what the recovered-voice novel was doing arrived after the fiction, giving a name and a discipline to the practice of narrating around an archival silence. Theory here followed art rather than leading it.
entries.example: Saidiya Hartman's concept of critical fabulation, set out in Venus in Two Acts (2008), articulated the method of straining against the archive's limits while keeping the silence visible, a discipline novelists had already been practising.
entries.application: Use the theory as a tool rather than a mandate, drawing on the discipline of narrating a gap without filling it dishonestly, while remembering the fiction found the method first.

entries.name: The Contemporary Literary Boom
entries.description: The contemporary literary boom: prestige and prizes disproportionate to the genre's market share.
entries.principle: The early twenty-first century saw the literary historical novel achieve unusual prestige, winning major prizes and critical seriousness disproportionate to its share of the market. The genre that critics once patronised became a leading form of the literary novel.
entries.example: Hilary Mantel's Cromwell novels, beginning with Wolf Hall (2009), won successive Booker Prizes and marked the arrival of the historical novel at the centre of literary fiction.
entries.application: Write into a moment when the form commands serious attention, and hold your work to the standard that prestige implies, while remembering the popular traditions that the literary boom sits alongside rather than above.

entries.name: The Neo-Victorian and the Self-Aware Past
entries.description: The neo-Victorian strand reads the nineteenth century through present concerns and its own silences.
entries.principle: A distinct contemporary strand reconstructs the nineteenth century with deliberate modern awareness, reading the period through present concerns and often through its own gaps and silences. The past becomes a mirror the book knowingly holds up.
entries.example: A. S. Byatt's Possession (1990) and Sarah Waters's Victorian novels reconstruct the era while foregrounding what it repressed, using a modern vantage to recover what the period's own record obscured.
entries.application: If you write the recent, well-documented past, decide how openly your modern perspective operates, and use the neo-Victorian mode's self-awareness to recover silences rather than merely to demonstrate hindsight.

entries.name: The Adaptation Economy
entries.description: The adaptation economy shapes what gets written, the costume drama a dominant public face.
entries.principle: The historical novel has long fed a prestige screen tradition, and the modern adaptation economy shapes what gets written, bought and remembered, since the costume drama and the prestige series are a dominant public face of the genre. The relationship between page and screen is now part of the form's history.
entries.example: Major historical novels are routinely optioned and adapted, and the prestige television era has made the screen historical, from long-running costume dramas to literary adaptations, a primary way audiences meet the genre.
entries.application: Understand that your historical novel enters an ecosystem shaped by adaptation, and while writing to the page's strengths, recognise how the screen tradition conditions readers' expectations of the period you reconstruct.

entries.name: From the Nation's Becoming to the Record's Silence
entries.description: The genre's arc: from how the nation became itself to who the record left out.
entries.principle: The arc of the genre's history is a turn in its central question, from the nineteenth century's how did the nation become itself to the late-twentieth and twenty-first century's who did the record leave out, and what do we owe them. The form moved from celebrating the powerful past to recovering the erased one.
entries.example: The distance from Scott's and Sienkiewicz's national romances to Morrison's Beloved and the postcolonial novel measures a whole shift in what the historical novel is for, from foundation myth to restitution.
entries.application: Locate your own book on this arc, knowing whether you are narrating a nation's becoming, recovering a silenced life, or something between, and understand that the choice places you in a long argument about what the genre owes the past.

entries.name: The Drive to Inhabit Other Times
entries.description: The historical imagination begins in the human impulse to inhabit times one did not live.
entries.principle: The historical imagination begins in a basic human impulse to inhabit times one did not live, an act of mental time travel that fiction extends and disciplines. Understanding the appeal is the first step to serving and interrogating it rather than merely indulging it.
entries.example: The persistent popularity of the historical novel across two centuries testifies to a durable wish to experience the past from inside, a wish the genre both satisfies and complicates.
entries.application: Ask what your reader is really seeking in the past, immersion, escape, understanding, or reckoning, and shape the book to that motive rather than assuming the mere pastness of the setting is the attraction.

entries.name: Nostalgia and the Sanitised Past
entries.description: Nostalgia sands the discomfort off the past; the novelist must choose to gratify it or resist it.
entries.principle: Nostalgia is a powerful and genuinely bittersweet emotion, and recent psychology suggests it can serve meaning and continuity, but as a lens on history it tends to sand off discomfort and produce a past cleaner than the real one. The historical novelist must decide whether to gratify nostalgia or to resist it.
entries.example: A period rendered as a warm, ordered lost world flatters a longing the reader brings, but the same period's documented squalor, cruelty or precariousness is what the sanitised version omits.
entries.application: Notice where your reconstruction is smoothing the past into comfort, and decide consciously whether the book indulges nostalgia or complicates it, since the sanitised past is a false claim however pleasant.

entries.name: Collective Memory
entries.description: Collective memory is socially constructed; the novel intervenes in it, not in a neutral record.
entries.principle: Societies remember collectively through shared frameworks that shape what individuals recall and how, so the past a culture carries is socially constructed rather than a sum of private memories. The historical novel intervenes in this collective memory rather than in a neutral record.
entries.example: Maurice Halbwachs argued that memory is structured by social frameworks, so that what a group remembers is organised by its present needs and institutions rather than preserved intact from the past.
entries.application: Recognise that your book enters a contested field of collective memory, and decide whether you are reinforcing the received communal version of an event or challenging it, since either way you are shaping what a culture remembers.

entries.name: Memory Is Reconstruction, Not Recording
entries.description: Memory is reconstruction, not recording, carrying its fallibility into eyewitness sources.
entries.principle: Individual memory is reconstructive rather than a faithful recording, assembled anew each time and vulnerable to distortion, which matters both for how eyewitness sources were formed and for how the past is popularly remembered. The record's human origins carry memory's fallibility.
entries.example: Experimental psychology since Bartlett has shown that remembering reshapes the past toward expectation and present need, so a memoir or testimony is a reconstruction, not a playback.
entries.application: Treat memory-based sources as reconstructions shaped after the fact, and where a character recalls the past, render memory's real unreliability rather than presenting recollection as accurate retrieval.

entries.name: Presentism as a Cognitive Bias
entries.description: Presentism as a cognitive default; seeing the past as alien takes active effort.
entries.principle: Humans spontaneously project present assumptions, values and knowledge onto the past, so presentism is not merely a scholarly error but a default of cognition the writer must actively counter. The past does not naturally appear alien; it takes effort to see it as it was.
entries.example: Readers and writers alike instinctively expect historical people to share modern intuitions about the self, morality and causation, and the effort of reconstruction is largely the effort to suspend that expectation.
entries.application: Treat presentism as a bias to be worked against continually, building period assumptions deliberately and checking your characters' minds for the modern defaults that slip in when attention lapses.

entries.name: Hindsight Bias and the Illusion of Inevitability
entries.description: Hindsight bias makes the past look inevitable; the task is to restore its genuine contingency.
entries.principle: In retrospect the past looks inevitable, its outcomes obvious, because hindsight bias reorganises what we know once we know how things turned out. The historical novelist's task is to restore the genuine contingency the participants experienced.
entries.example: Research on hindsight bias, associated with Baruch Fischhoff, shows that once an outcome is known people overestimate how predictable it was, which is why documented history reads as fated.
entries.application: Recover the real uncertainty your historical figures faced, dramatising the alternatives that seemed open to them, so the reader feels the contingency that hindsight has erased from the record.

entries.name: The Empathy Question
entries.description: Whether we can feel what an alien era felt is uncertain; the empathy claim should be made modestly.
entries.principle: Whether we can truly feel what people of a radically different era felt is genuinely uncertain, and the claim that fiction lets us do so should be made modestly. The historical novel can foster understanding, but the assumption of full empathic access to an alien mentality overreaches the evidence.
entries.example: The popular defence of historical fiction as a machine for cross-temporal empathy rests on a psychology of fiction-and-empathy that has had its own replication difficulties, so the claim is better made as understanding than as felt identity.
entries.application: Aim to make an alien mentality comprehensible rather than claiming the reader can fully feel it, and treat the empathy the genre offers as partial and constructed rather than as transparent access to a vanished mind.

entries.name: Historical Distance and the Uncanny
entries.description: The productive zone is the uncanny middle: recognisable humans holding unrecognisable assumptions.
entries.principle: The past is experienced as both familiar and alien, and the productive zone of the historical imagination is the uncanny middle where recognisable humans hold unrecognisable assumptions. Too much familiarity collapses into costume-modern; too much strangeness loses the reader.
entries.example: A period that feels entirely relatable has usually been modernised, while one that feels wholly alien resists engagement, and the strongest historical fiction holds both, the human and the strange, at once.
entries.application: Calibrate the distance so your reader recognises the humanity and feels the strangeness together, resisting both the comfort of a past just like now and the alienation of a past with no point of entry.

entries.name: The Craving for Authenticity
entries.description: Readers crave the real, but authenticity is an effect of craft, not the same as the real.
entries.principle: Readers of historical fiction crave a sense of the real, and that craving is a psychological fact the genre both serves and can exploit. Authenticity is largely an effect produced by craft, so the feeling of the real is not the same as the real.
entries.example: The persuasive texture of a well-researched novel produces a conviction of authenticity that a reader experiences as access to the past, though it is an artefact of selection and technique.
entries.application: Understand that you are producing an effect of authenticity rather than delivering the past itself, and use the reader's craving responsibly, since the more convincing the effect, the greater the trust you are being given.

entries.name: Escape and Confrontation
entries.description: The past read for escape or for confrontation; knowing which clarifies what the book owes.
entries.principle: The past is read for two opposite motives, escape from the present and confrontation with a truth the present avoids, and a historical novel usually leans toward one. Knowing which motive your book serves clarifies what it owes the reader and the record.
entries.example: The same historical setting can be a comforting elsewhere or a mirror for present injustice, and the difference lies in whether the book invites the reader to flee the present or to face it.
entries.application: Decide whether your book offers escape or confrontation, and align its handling of comfort, difficulty and moral pressure accordingly, rather than promising one and delivering the other.

entries.name: The Usable Past and Identity
entries.description: The usable past feeds a hunger for roots that can shade from meaning into myth-making.
entries.principle: People seek in the past a usable inheritance, roots, ancestry and belonging, and historical fiction feeds this hunger for a story of where one comes from. The pull is powerful and can shade from meaning into myth-making.
entries.example: The appeal of ancestral and heritage narratives shows how readers use the past to locate themselves, which gives the genre real emotional force and a real temptation toward flattering origin stories.
entries.application: Recognise the identity-hunger your book may feed, and decide whether you are offering genuine inheritance or a comforting myth of origins, since the usable past can console or deceive.

entries.name: Postmemory and Inherited Trauma
entries.description: Postmemory: the memory of atrocity transmitted to descendants who did not experience it.
entries.principle: The memory of atrocity is transmitted across generations to those who did not experience it, shaping descendants through inherited images and stories. This transmitted relationship to a traumatic past is a distinct psychological condition the historical novel of recent atrocity engages.
entries.example: Marianne Hirsch's concept of postmemory describes how the children of survivors relate to events they did not live but that dominate their formation, a dynamic central to fiction of the Holocaust and other recent catastrophes.
entries.application: When you write a recent atrocity with living descendants, recognise that you are entering a field of inherited memory, and weigh what your reconstruction does to those who carry the event without having lived it.

entries.name: Progress and Decline as Frames
entries.description: Progress and decline as master frames that flatten a period into a direction.
entries.principle: The historical imagination is shaped by master frames of progress and of decline, either of which can distort a period into a stage on the way up or a fall from a golden age. Both are cognitive shortcuts that flatten the past to a direction.
entries.example: A whiggish reading treats the past as the imperfect prelude to an enlightened present, while a declinist reading mourns a lost order, and each imposes a trajectory the period itself did not experience.
entries.application: Notice which master frame your book leans on, and resist letting progress or decline predetermine the meaning of your period, so the past is rendered as lived rather than as a stage in a story of rise or fall.

entries.name: Condemning the Dead
entries.description: Condemning the dead is self-congratulation that substitutes for comprehending them.
entries.principle: Readers derive a moral satisfaction from judging the past and feeling superior to its people, a form of self-congratulation that flattens historical understanding. The reflex to condemn the dead can substitute for the harder work of comprehending them.
entries.example: A narrative that invites the reader to look down on benighted ancestors offers an easy virtue, whereas one that makes a repellent period-accurate worldview comprehensible demands more of the reader and teaches more.
entries.application: Resist building the book to let the reader feel superior to the past, and aim instead for comprehension of why decent people held indecent views, since condemnation is easy and understanding is the genre's real work.

entries.name: The Just-World Distortion
entries.description: The just-world distortion narrates history as suffering deserved and outcomes earned.
entries.principle: The tendency to believe the world is fundamentally just biases how people narrate history, encouraging stories in which suffering is deserved or redeemed and outcomes are earned. This distortion falsifies a past full of unearned catastrophe and unpunished wrong.
entries.example: A historical narrative that quietly supplies moral order, punishing the wicked and rewarding the good against the documented record, gratifies the just-world bias at the cost of truth.
entries.application: Guard against imposing moral order the record does not support, and let your history include the unearned and the unresolved, since the just-world reflex will otherwise smuggle a false justice into the past.

entries.name: The Weaponised Golden Age
entries.description: The weaponised golden age: nostalgia deployed to authorise present agendas.
entries.principle: Nostalgia for an imagined golden age is a recurring political force, and historical narratives are routinely deployed to authorise present agendas through a flattering or aggrieved past. The historical novelist works with material that others use as a weapon.
entries.example: Invocations of a lost national greatness or a defiled heritage show how a mythologised past is mobilised politically, which is the national-romance impulse turned to present ends.
entries.application: Be aware that your reconstruction of a period enters a landscape where the past is politically contested, and take responsibility for whether your book underwrites a golden-age myth or complicates it.

entries.name: Counterfactual Thinking
entries.description: Counterfactual thinking, the what-if reflex the alternate-history mode feeds.
entries.principle: Humans habitually imagine how things might have gone otherwise, and this counterfactual reflex underlies both ordinary regret and the alternate-history mode. The psychology of the what-if is the appetite the counterfactual historical novel feeds.
entries.example: The ease with which readers entertain a world where a battle or an election went the other way reflects a deep cognitive tendency to simulate alternatives, which alternate history formalises.
entries.application: If you work in the counterfactual, understand that you are engaging a natural mental habit, and make the alternative argue about the real outcome it displaces rather than merely indulging the pleasure of the what-if.

entries.name: The Narrative Imposition
entries.description: The mind imposes narrative on history; the novel should know it shapes rather than finds a story.
entries.principle: History as lived is not a story, but the human mind imposes narrative shape on it, selecting beginnings, middles and ends that the events did not contain. The historical novel is the most explicit form of this emplotment, and it should know that it is shaping rather than finding a story.
entries.example: Hayden White argued that historical writing gives events a narrative form, an emplotment, that is a construction rather than a property of the past, so the story is added by the teller.
entries.application: Remember that the shape you give your history is imposed, not discovered, and choose your emplotment consciously, aware that the beginning and ending you select are claims about meaning the events themselves did not make.

entries.name: Why Atrocity Fascinates
entries.description: Atrocity's real fascination is a fact for the writer to handle, not a licence to exploit.
entries.principle: Dark historical material exerts a real fascination, and the psychology of that attraction, part horror, part moral seriousness, part appetite for spectacle, is something the writer of atrocity must understand rather than simply exploit. The pull is a fact to be handled, not a licence.
entries.example: The enduring readership for fiction of war, slavery and genocide reflects a mix of legitimate reckoning and less creditable appetite, and the same book can serve either depending on how it is built.
entries.application: Acknowledge the fascination your dark material exerts and design against its exploitation, ensuring the book engages the reader's moral seriousness rather than feeding an appetite for suffering as spectacle.

entries.name: The Pleasure of Recognition
entries.description: The pleasure of recognition rewards familiarity but pulls the book toward the clichéd.
entries.principle: A distinct pleasure of historical fiction is recognition, the reader's satisfaction at meeting a period detail they already know, which rewards familiarity but can pull the book toward the expected and the clichéd. The recognisable is pleasant and can be lazy.
entries.example: The comfort a reader takes in encountering the famous landmarks of a period, the known names and the stock images, is real but risks reducing the past to its most circulated surfaces.
entries.application: Offer some recognition to orient the reader, but do not build the period from its clichés, and use the pleasure of the familiar as an entry point to the unfamiliar rather than as the substance of the reconstruction.

entries.name: The History of the Self
entries.description: Interiority has a history; a period mind is a different structure of subjectivity, not just different views.
entries.principle: Personhood and interiority have a history, and people of other eras understood the self, the emotions and the inner life in ways that differ from modern assumptions. Reconstructing a period mind means reconstructing a different structure of subjectivity, not just different opinions.
entries.example: Scholarship on the history of emotions and of the self argues that categories such as privacy, individuality and even particular feelings are historically variable, so an ancient or medieval interior is not a modern one in period dress.
entries.application: Research how your period understood the self and the emotions, and build your characters' inner lives on that structure, resisting the assumption that only their circumstances, not their psychology, differed from ours.

entries.name: Anachronism as Comfort
entries.description: Anachronism of mind persists partly because a familiar past comforts the reader.
entries.principle: Readers often resist a genuinely alien past and prefer a familiar one, so anachronism of mind persists partly because it comforts. The pressure to modernise the past comes not only from the writer's laziness but from the reader's wish to recognise themselves in it.
entries.example: A protagonist given modern sensibilities in a brutal period is easier to love, which is precisely why such characters are common, and why the truer, stranger figure is a harder sell.
entries.application: Recognise that resistance to an alien past may come from the reader's comfort as much as from your craft, and decide how far you will meet that comfort, knowing that the modernised past is the easier and the falser one.

entries.name: Fiction as Vicarious Witness
entries.description: Fiction as vicarious witness, carrying ethical weight and the risk of false intimacy with suffering.
entries.principle: Reading historical fiction can function as a form of vicarious witness, a way of standing before events one could not attend, which carries both a real ethical weight and a risk of false intimacy with suffering one has not shared. The sense of having witnessed is powerful and partly illusory.
entries.example: A novel of atrocity can leave a reader feeling they have borne witness, an experience that can deepen moral seriousness or can flatter a spectator into mistaking reading for testimony.
entries.application: Weigh what it means to offer the reader vicarious witness, and build the book so that the experience deepens responsibility rather than granting a false claim to have shared or understood the suffering depicted.

entries.name: The Authenticity Paradox
entries.description: The authenticity paradox: the more immersive the reconstruction feels, the more heavily constructed it is.
entries.principle: The more immersive and convincing a reconstruction feels, the more heavily constructed it actually is, because the effect of the real is produced by intense selection and technique. Immersion is not transparency; it is the most artful kind of making.
entries.example: The densest, most convincing historical worlds are the product of the most deliberate authorial choices about what to include and exclude, so their seeming naturalness is their greatest artifice.
entries.application: Do not mistake your own immersive effect for fidelity, and remember that the reader's strongest sense of the real marks the point where your construction is most complete, and most in need of honest checking.

entries.name: Whose Past Gets Imagined
entries.description: Whose past gets imagined reflects present power and interest, not the past's own weight.
entries.principle: Historical attention is unevenly distributed, and which periods, places and peoples get imagined in fiction reflects present power and interest rather than the past's own weight. The map of what the genre reconstructs is itself a fact about the present.
entries.example: The heavy concentration of historical fiction on a handful of familiar Western periods, and the relative neglect of others, shows that the genre imagines selectively, following present attention rather than the past's actual scale.
entries.application: Notice what your choice of subject reflects about present attention, and recognise that reconstructing a neglected past is itself an intervention in the uneven distribution of who gets remembered.

entries.name: The Limits of the Historical Imagination
entries.description: Some of the past is genuinely unrecoverable; honesty about those limits is part of the discipline.
entries.principle: Some things about the past are genuinely unrecoverable, and honesty about those limits is part of the discipline, since several claims the genre makes for itself circulate with more confidence than the evidence supports. The historical imagination is powerful and bounded, and pretending otherwise is its characteristic overreach.
entries.example: The claims that fiction grants full empathic access to an alien mind, that immersion delivers the past transparently, and that reading atrocity constitutes witness are each stronger than the evidence warrants, and each is routinely asserted as settled.
entries.application: Defend the historical novel on the ground it can hold, that it disciplines the imagination toward understanding and complicates the record, rather than on inflated psychological claims, and let honest humility about what cannot be recovered be part of the book's integrity.

entries.name: The Fictional Witness
entries.description: An invented character is placed at a documented event so the reader can experience real history through a figure the author is free to move, feel and reveal, without altering the record's outcome.

examples.text: Cornwell inserts a fictional rifleman into the Peninsular War so a real campaign is felt through an invented soldier's eyes without bending its history.
Shaara witnesses Gettysburg through real commanders but leans on invented interiority to make documented positions humanly legible.
the fictional witness meets every landmark of an era, but the device tips into a tour of history rather than an experience of it.

entries.name: The Ordinary Person Swept Up
entries.description: A commonplace protagonist is caught by historical forces beyond their control, so vast events are measured by their cost to someone with no power over them.

examples.text: a physician-poet is carried through revolution and civil war, the upheaval measured by what it does to a private life.
Barry's young Dublin volunteer is swept into the First World War and the Easter Rising, powerless before both.
the ordinary lovers swept up in the attack are so subordinated to spectacle that the history swamps the people it should be measured by.

entries.name: The Servant's-Eye View
entries.description: Great events and great households are seen from below stairs, so the vantage of the powerless reconstructs a history the masters' record omits.

examples.text: Ishiguro's butler narrates a house at the centre of appeasement, his deference blinding him to the politics he serves.
Baker retells a familiar story from its servants, recovering the labour the original left invisible.
the downstairs vantage is present but softened into nostalgia, the real asymmetry of the household smoothed for comfort.

entries.name: The Real Person as Protagonist
entries.description: A documented historical figure is the centre of the novel, binding invention to evidence and staking the book on an interior imagined consistently with the record.

examples.text: Mantel builds Thomas Cromwell's undocumented interior in exhaustive depth while never moving the documented furniture of events.
Yourcenar reconstructs a Roman emperor as a dying man's letter, imagining an interior the record cannot supply.
Stone's Michelangelo is vivid but flattened toward a modern genius-hero, the period mind subordinated to the biography.

entries.name: The Composite Character
entries.description: Several real people are combined into one invented figure, a legitimate compression that nonetheless contradicts the record and works best when the author knows and, where it matters, declares it.

examples.text: Lampedusa's Prince distils a class and a moment into one figure drawn from his own Sicilian ancestry.
the composite hero absorbs deeds and chronology from many sources, and the undeclared compression hardens into false history.
a composite rebellion and a foreign witness merge real figures into a shape the record did not hold.

entries.name: The Traveller Who Meets Everyone
entries.description: A single character improbably crosses paths with every notable figure of an age, an efficient tour of a period that risks reducing history to a parade of cameos.

examples.text: Doctorow threads fictional families through a crowd of real early-century figures, using the artifice knowingly as collage.

examples.work: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay
examples.text: the comics-age panorama is dazzling but leans on the hero brushing every landmark of the era.
the protagonist's collision with every historical moment is the whole conceit, and history becomes a backdrop for coincidence.

entries.name: The Child in History
entries.description: A child narrator or protagonist reports a period accurately while misreading it, so the reader grasps what the child cannot and exposition arrives as dramatic irony.

examples.text: a girl in Nazi Germany registers the regime's cruelty through a child's partial understanding.
Ballard's boy in occupied Shanghai sees a war whose meaning outruns him.

examples.work: The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas
examples.text: the child's-eye innocence about a death camp strains plausibility to the point of falsifying the history it depicts.

entries.name: The Last Survivor
entries.description: An aged narrator recalls events from the far end of a life, framing the past as memory and licensing both the authority of the witness and the distortions of recollection.

examples.work: All the Light We Cannot See
examples.text: Doerr's braided recollection reaches back to the war from the vantage of what survived it.
Frazier's Civil War is filtered through memory and return, the survivor's account shaping the telling.
the aged survivor's framing recollection sentimentalises a class-stratified disaster into a single remembered romance.

entries.name: The Outsider Guide
entries.description: A traveller, foreigner or newcomer serves as the reader's proxy, licensing explanation because the character genuinely does not know the world they are entering.

examples.text: Clavell's stranded Englishman lets the reader learn feudal Japan alongside a man who must learn it to survive.
the young novice Adso narrates a monastery whose intrigues he only half understands, guiding the reader through them.
the outsider guide becomes the story's centre, displacing the people whose world he was meant to open.

entries.name: The Sympathetic Anachronism
entries.description: A protagonist is given modern sensibilities in a pre-modern world so the reader can like them, the most common and most falsifying form of presentism.

examples.text: the deliberately anachronistic hero is charming, and the film owns the anachronism, but the period mind is entirely modern.
the heroine's modern environmental and egalitarian sensibility is projected onto a figure and a moment that held neither.
the Tudor women are given contemporary attitudes to choice and self that the period foreclosed, dissolving the very constraints that make their story tragic.

entries.name: The Figure Between Two Worlds
entries.description: A character straddles two cultures, sides or eras, and their divided loyalty dramatises a historical collision from inside rather than from one bank of it.

examples.text: Achebe's Okonkwo stands at the fracture of Igbo society and colonial arrival, embodying a world coming apart.
Ghosh's crossings of caste, race and empire put characters between worlds the opium trade is forcing together.
the between-worlds hero is romantic but flattens the historical collision into a love story across it.

entries.name: The Found Manuscript
entries.description: The novel presents itself as a recovered document, motivating the telling and foregrounding how the past is transmitted, at the cost of added distance from the events.

examples.text: Eco frames the tale as a translated recovered chronicle, layering transmission over the mystery.
the nested found documents build atmosphere but slow the narrative under their own apparatus.
the memoir frame asserts documentary authority the contested facts cannot fully support.

entries.name: The Dual Timeline
entries.description: A present-day strand, often a researcher, is braided with the historical one, so the act of recovering the past becomes part of the story and its uncertainties are dramatised.

examples.text: Byatt sets modern scholars chasing a Victorian secret, making research itself the plot.
Brooks tracks a real manuscript's survival across centuries through a present-day conservator.
the framing present adds a sentimental layer that dilutes rather than deepens the past it recovers.

entries.name: The Generational Relay
entries.description: The story passes like a baton from one generation to the next, so a period's meaning accumulates across the lives it shapes rather than resting in a single arc.

examples.text: Gyasi hands the narrative down two branches of a family from eighteenth-century Ghana to the present, each chapter a link in a chain of consequence.
McCullough's saga carries an Australian family across decades so history is felt as inheritance.
the generational relay is powerful but complicated by the documented disputes over its factual claims.

entries.name: The Chronicler Within
entries.description: A scribe, historian or record-keeper inside the story writes the very account we read, dramatising the making of the record and its biases within the fiction.

examples.text: Graves's emperor writes his secret history, and his stated candour is itself a device the reader must weigh.
Pears sets four narrators each writing their account of the same Restoration events, foregrounding the record's unreliability.
the in-world narrator recovers a silenced voice compellingly but asserts documentary access the biblical record cannot ground.

entries.name: The Unreliable Historical Narrator
entries.description: The teller of the historical tale is compromised, self-serving or mistaken, so the reader must read past them to the events, mirroring the historian's work on a biased source.

examples.text: Stevens's self-deceiving narration conceals the politics of the house even from himself, and the reader reads around him.
McEwan makes the narrator's own fiction the instrument of a lie, indicting the consoling version of events.
the naive narrator's unreliability is played for whimsy rather than for any purchase on the history he crosses.

entries.name: The Reconstructing Investigator
entries.description: A character pieces the past together from fragments, and the detective work models how history is actually assembled from partial and contradictory evidence.

examples.text: Harris reconstructs the Dreyfus affair through the officer who uncovers it, the evidence assembled before the reader.
Waters's plot turns on the slow reconstruction of a hidden Victorian history.
the historical reconstruction is propulsive but rests on claims the record does not support and asserts as fact.

entries.name: The Time-Bridging Object
entries.description: A single artefact passes through eras or anchors a period, concentrating history in a thing the reader can hold onto across the sweep.

examples.text: a real Haggadah's physical traces open each historical layer of its survival.
an instrument carries the film across centuries and continents, each owner a period.

examples.work: The Girl with a Pearl Earring
examples.text: the painting anchors the period beautifully but the invented backstory strains against the sparse record of the real work.

entries.name: The Eyewitness to the Turning Point
entries.description: A character is present at the precise hinge of history, so the famous moment is delivered through one person's limited, embodied experience rather than an overview.

examples.text: Mantel delivers Anne Boleyn's fall through Cromwell's immediate, partial vantage.
Golding stages a shipboard death as the hinge the whole narrative turns on, seen through one baffled diarist.
the eyewitness vantage is repeatedly abandoned for the aerial spectacle, losing the human scale it promised.

entries.name: The Provincial Drawn to the Centre
entries.description: An outsider from the margins is pulled into the court, capital or centre of power, and their unfamiliarity lets the reader learn the centre's rules as the character does.

examples.text: Catton's newcomer arrives in a gold-rush town whose web of interests he must learn to survive.
Sienkiewicz's characters move from the margins into Nero's Rome, the corrupt centre seen through fresher eyes.
the court is the whole world and no outsider vantage grounds it, so its rules are asserted rather than learned.

entries.name: The Interpreter Between Powers
entries.description: A translator or go-between stands at the seam of two powers, and their mediating position exposes how much of history is made in the gap between what is said and what is understood.

examples.text: Endō's interpreters and apostates mediate between Portuguese missionaries and the Japanese state, the translation itself a site of betrayal.
Adichie's characters mediate between worlds as Biafra collapses, standing between combatants and languages.
the interpreter figure is romanticised, the hard political work of mediation dissolved into image.

entries.name: The Epistolary Reconstruction
entries.description: The story is told through invented letters, diaries or documents, so the period's own forms of writing carry the narrative and imitate the texture of the archive.

examples.text: Walker's letters reconstruct a Black woman's early-century life from inside her own written voice.

examples.work: The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society
examples.text: the postwar letters rebuild an occupation through correspondence, though the tone runs toward the cosy.
where it leans on documentary framing it lends its Lost Cause content a false authority, a caution rather than a model.

entries.name: The Community as Protagonist
entries.description: A village, town or people rather than an individual is the true subject, so the history is carried by a collective whose fate is the story.

examples.text: Brooks makes a plague village that quarantines itself the real protagonist of the book.
Unsworth's slave-ship and its improvised colony function as a collective subject Unsworth indicts.
the village-as-protagonist frame is warm but the period pressures on the community are softened toward fable.

entries.name: The Past That Will Not Stay Buried
entries.description: History returns as haunting, literal or figurative, so an unresolved atrocity or loss presses on the living and dramatises the record's refusal to close.

examples.text: Morrison makes slavery's unmourned dead return as a presence, so the past that the record silenced becomes physically insistent.
O'Farrell lets a child's death haunt a household and, obliquely, a famous play the record barely connects to it.
the haunting device is affecting but the historical texture is thin, the period incidental to the ghost.

entries.name: The Return to the Ruined Homeland
entries.description: A character comes back to a place transformed or destroyed by history, and the gap between memory and ruin measures what the period has done.

examples.text: Ondaatje's characters return, broken, to landscapes the war has emptied of meaning.
Lee's Korean family measures decades of occupation and diaspora against a homeland they can never simply return to.
the return-to-the-land epic gestures at Stolen Generations history but subordinates it to romance and spectacle.

entries.name: The Known-Death March
entries.description: The reader knows a documented figure is doomed, and the narrative moves steadily toward the death, converting suspense into dread and the pleasure of anticipation into grief.

examples.text: Mantel writes toward Cromwell's execution the reader has awaited across three books, the doom gathering weight.
the adaptation sustains the same gathering inevitability, every scene shadowed by the block.
the known ending hovers but the film's surfaces so dominate that the coming death registers faintly.

entries.name: The Countdown to a Famous Event
entries.description: The plot ticks toward a documented event whose date the reader knows, so ordinary scenes acquire tension from the calendar bearing down on them.

examples.text: Mantel's revolutionaries advance toward the Terror the reader knows will consume them.
the hours before the documented disaster are charged precisely because the outcome is known and approaching.
the volcano's countdown is the only real engine, the human story thin beneath the coming eruption.

entries.name: The Secret Behind the Record
entries.description: The novel posits a hidden cause or truth behind documented events, on the condition that it never contradicts the known facts, inventing into the gaps rather than against them.

examples.text: Pears fits a concealed truth precisely into the documented gaps of Restoration Oxford.
Carr threads an invented investigation through a densely real 1896 New York without dislodging its facts.
the hidden history is propulsive but rests on claims the record does not support and asserts as fact.

entries.name: The Eve of Catastrophe
entries.description: The book dwells on the last ordinary day before a known disaster, and the reader's foreknowledge turns quotidian detail into elegy.

examples.text: Visconti lingers over a Sicilian aristocracy on the eve of its supersession, the ball a long farewell to a dying order.
Némirovsky records the last hours of a peace her own present was ending, the ordinary about to be swept away.
the eve-of-disaster device works but flattens a class-stratified catastrophe into a single remembered romance.

entries.name: The Survivor's Reckoning
entries.description: After the documented catastrophe the book stays with those who lived, so its meaning is measured in aftermath, grief and the labour of going on rather than in the event itself.

examples.work: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
examples.text: Flanagan follows his prisoners of war long past the railway, the survival more harrowing than the ordeal.
Lee measures decades of occupation and diaspora in what the survivors carry forward.
the reckoning is affecting but resolves the historical trauma into a single act of personal reconciliation.

entries.name: The What-If Hinge
entries.description: Within a realist frame the book dramatises a moment history could have turned, recovering the genuine contingency the participants felt without leaving the documented outcome.

examples.text: Towles keeps alive the sense that his count's fate, and Russia's, might have gone otherwise.
Vidal restores the contingency of the early republic through a narrator who saw its outcomes as anything but settled.

examples.work: The Man in the High Castle
examples.text: the hinge is literalised into full counterfactual, which belongs to the alternate-history hand-off rather than the realist frame.

entries.name: Parallel Lives
entries.description: Two figures whose paths mirror or diverge across a period let the book measure history by the different fates it deals to comparable people.

examples.text: Whitehead sets escape against recapture so two trajectories map the machinery of slavery.
the immigrant father's rise and the son's moral fall are braided across two historical periods.
the two sisters' parallel fates are schematic, the mirror too neatly drawn.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The Rise and Fall
entries.description: The arc of a figure, family or empire climbing to power and then losing it gives the historical novel a shape the record often supplies, at the risk of a mechanical trajectory.

examples.text: the adaptation charts the Julio-Claudian ascents and ruins as a single dynastic machine of rise and fall.
McCullough builds the late Republic as a study in how power is climbed and cannot be held.
the rise-and-fall shape is satisfying but the invented emperor plot bends the record to melodrama.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The End of an Order
entries.description: A whole world ends in real time on the page, its assumptions dying with it, so the reader watches a way of life become history.

examples.text: Lampedusa renders the death of a Sicilian aristocratic order as a class watching itself become the past.
the fall of the plantation South is rendered as an order's death, though the book mourns a world built on slavery, which this card names.
the end of the samurai order is elegised through an outsider whose centrality distorts the history.

entries.name: The Past as Investigation
entries.description: The narrative reconstructs a historical truth as an inquiry, modelling how history is assembled from partial evidence, distinct from the crime hand-off in that the quarry is understanding rather than a culprit.

examples.text: Byatt's scholars assemble a Victorian secret from letters and diaries, the research itself the plot.
the player reconstructs a murder and a manuscript in a sixteenth-century abbey, the game explicitly about how records are made and misread.
the documentary investigation builds atmosphere but slows under the weight of its own nested apparatus.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The Doomed Cause
entries.description: The characters serve a rebellion or movement the reader knows will fail, so their commitment is coloured throughout by an outcome they cannot see.

examples.text: Gibbon's Scottish community is carried toward a war and a modernity that will end its way of life.
Barry's volunteers serve causes, Irish and imperial, that the reader knows will betray them.
the doomed cause is vivid but the film compresses and reshapes the record enough to distort the history it mourns.

entries.name: The Odyssey Across a Period
entries.description: A long journey carries the protagonist and the reader across a period's landscape and social range, letting one route survey a whole historical world.

examples.text: Frazier walks a deserter home across a disintegrating Confederacy, the route a survey of its collapse.
Portis sends a girl across a frontier whose law, violence and commerce she meets stage by stage.
the journeys across eras are ambitious but the historical strands are thinned by the film's cross-cutting.

entries.name: The Trial as Spine
entries.description: A documented trial provides the book's structure, its testimony and verdict organising the history and its contested truths.

examples.work: I, Tituba, Black Witch of Salem
examples.text: Condé builds around the Salem proceedings to recover the voice they silenced.
Harris organises the Dreyfus affair around its trials and their manufactured evidence.
powerful as drama, but its Salem is shaped to a mid-century allegory that bends the historical particulars.

entries.name: The Siege
entries.description: A bounded community under prolonged historical assault concentrates a period's pressures into one place and a countdown of dwindling resources and resolve.

examples.text: Farrell traps a colonial garrison in the 1857 rebellion and lets the siege dismantle its every imperial certainty.
the ruins of Stalingrad compress the war into a bounded duel of snipers.
the siege is stylised into myth, the historical Thermopylae dissolved into spectacle and propaganda.

entries.name: The Plague Community
entries.description: A population meets an epidemic or disaster, and the community's response, quarantine, scapegoating, sacrifice, reveals its values under mortal pressure.

examples.text: Brooks makes a plague village that quarantines itself the real protagonist of the book.

examples.work: A Journal of the Plague Year
examples.text: Defoe's reconstructed account of 1665, written decades later, is an early model of the disaster community as history.
the cholera epidemic frames a marriage drama more than it examines the community it strikes.

entries.name: The Inheritance of History
entries.description: A consequence, debt or wound is passed down through a family, so a documented historical harm reaches the present through the generations it deformed.

examples.text: Gyasi carries the inheritance of the slave trade down two family lines to the present.
Condé follows a Bambara family as slavery, Islam and empire reshape what each generation inherits.
the inheritance structure is landmark television, though the source's factual disputes shadow its claims.

entries.name: The Convergence
entries.description: Multiple separate strands are drawn together at a documented historical event, so the moment gathers a cross-section of a society into one place.

examples.text: Catton converges a dozen fates on a gold-rush town's linked crimes and fortunes.
the film converges its fictional and real figures on the era's flashpoints.
the strands converge at Waterloo but the history is flattened to a backdrop for the heroine's rise.

entries.name: The Circling Frame
entries.description: The story opens and closes on a framing present, and the return completes a meaning the historical core could not deliver alone, though a weak frame merely delays the past.

examples.text: McEwan's framing return reveals the whole narrative as an act of guilty reconstruction.
Hartley's aged narrator returns to the summer that broke him, the frame essential to the meaning.
the modern-cemetery frame adds sentiment the war narrative did not need and slightly cheapens it.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The Wheel of Fortune
entries.description: A documented reversal of fortune, a fall from favour or a sudden elevation, structures the narrative around the period's own sense of fate and the precariousness of standing.

examples.text: Towles turns a sentence of house arrest into a long study of fortune's reversals within four walls.
Kubrick charts an adventurer's rise into and precipitous fall out of the eighteenth-century gentry.
the court's reversals are sharp but the film's knowing anachronism keeps the period at arm's length.

entries.name: The Race Against a Known Outcome
entries.description: A character strives to achieve or prevent something the reader knows the result of, so the tension lies not in the outcome but in the cost and the manner of reaching it.

examples.text: the reader knows the rescue's scale, and the suspense is in each life saved against the machinery of murder.
Higgins runs a documented-seeming wartime plot whose failure the reader can infer, the tension in its unfolding.
the abolition campaign's known victory drains the film's suspense, which it never quite replaces with cost.

entries.name: The Buried Atrocity Surfaces
entries.description: A suppressed historical crime surfaces within the plot, and its uncovering dramatises the record's active silences and the labour of recovery.

examples.text: Whitehead's reform-school graves surface a real, long-hidden atrocity through the plot's excavation of it.
Adichie brings the suppressed scale of the Biafran famine into the foreground of the narrative.
the film gestures at Stolen Generations history but subordinates the surfacing atrocity to romance and spectacle.

entries.name: The Message Too Late
entries.description: The period's real information lag becomes plot, as a letter, order or warning arrives after it could matter, the delay generating a tragedy the modern reader must be made to feel.

examples.text: O'Brian's ships act on orders and intelligence weeks stale, the lag shaping every decision.

examples.work: The Charge of the Light Brigade
examples.text: a miscarried order sends the brigade to slaughter, the period's fatal chain of command laid bare.
a misdirected letter drives the plot but the period lag serves romance rather than history.

entries.name: Mistaken Identity in Period
entries.description: An impostor or misidentification exploits a period's limited means of verifying who a person is, a structure the pre-modern record makes newly plausible.

examples.text: Lewis builds the sixteenth-century impostor case on exactly the period's inability to fix identity.
the film makes the slowness of proof in a village the very ground of the deception.
the same structure transplanted to the American Civil War loosens the period logic that made the original credible.

entries.name: The Reconstructed Massacre
entries.description: The book builds toward or around a documented mass killing, and the trope foregrounds the craft question of how to render atrocity as history rather than as spectacle.

examples.text: McCarthy renders frontier slaughter with a bleak documentary refusal to redeem it.
the film insists on the duration and ordinariness of atrocity rather than staging it for effect.
Griffith's technically influential film reconstructs Reconstruction as a racist myth, the paradigm of history weaponised as spectacle.

entries.name: The Past Explains the Present
entries.description: A dual structure resolves when the historical strand reveals the cause of the present one, so recovery of the past becomes the plot's payoff rather than its frame.

examples.text: the buried Victorian history, once uncovered, reorganises everything the present strand appeared to be.

examples.work: The Thousand Autumns of Jacob de Zoet
examples.text: Mitchell lets a trading-post past account for the fates it sets in motion.
the past-explains-present structure moves emotionally but the period is decorative, incidental to the romance.

entries.name: Forbidden Love Across a Divide
entries.description: A love the period forbids, across class, faith, race or status, dramatises a social order by testing it, so the relationship's danger is the era's structure made personal.

examples.text: Levy sets desire against the absolute barriers of a Jamaican slave plantation, where the divide is law and violence.

examples.work: Snow Flower and the Secret Fan
examples.text: See renders bonds between women constrained by a nineteenth-century Chinese custom that leaves them almost no room to act.
the separated lovers are affecting, but the divide is circumstance rather than a period structure that tests them.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The Marriage of State
entries.description: A dynastic or political marriage subordinates the personal to the strategic, so a period's understanding of alliance, property and women's roles is enacted in a single arranged union.

examples.text: Penman builds the Wars of the Roses partly through marriages made and broken for advantage.
the Boleyn and Aragon marriages are shown as instruments of state on which lives and religions turn.
the political marriages of Mary Stuart are recast as teen romance, dissolving the statecraft that gave them meaning.

entries.name: The Reformer Ahead of Their Time
entries.description: A character pushes against their era's norms, and the trope's hazard is presentism, since a genuinely period reformer argued from within their own world's terms, not from ours.

examples.text: Kidd grounds its abolitionist sisters in the documented Grimké record and the religious language they actually used.
Unsworth's dissenting figures argue against the slave trade in the idioms their own century allowed.
the heroine's modern environmental and egalitarian creed is projected onto a figure and moment that held neither.

entries.name: The Loyal Retainer
entries.description: A servant, steward or soldier bound by loyalty to a master embodies a period's ideals of service and hierarchy, and the bond's strain exposes what that loyalty cost.

examples.text: the butler's absolute service to a compromised master is the film's quiet indictment of deference.
the ranker's loyalties up and down a rigid military hierarchy structure the soldier's world.
the retainer's loyalty is rendered as mutual affection, softening the real asymmetry of the arrangement.

entries.name: The Period-Normal Villain
entries.description: A character whose cruelty is simply their era's accepted normal forces the reader to confront a worldview the book need not endorse, and the craft is to render the conviction without a modern conscience.

examples.text: the Judge articulates a frontier philosophy of violence entirely coherent within its world's terms.
Jones's slaveholders, including a Black one, act on a system they experience as ordinary, which is the book's chilling point.
the slavers are drawn as simple monsters, which lets the audience off the harder recognition of an ordinary evil.

entries.name: The Woman Constrained by Her Era
entries.description: A woman's agency is bounded by her period's real limits on property, marriage, work and voice, and the drama lies in what she achieves or loses within constraints the book must not quietly lift.

examples.text: Fitzgerald renders women's circumscribed eighteenth-century lives with such precision that their small freedoms carry enormous weight.
Perry lets a Victorian widow's new latitude and its limits shape every choice she makes.
the Tudor women are given a modern latitude of choice the period foreclosed, dissolving the constraints that made their story tragic.

entries.name: The Enslaved Protagonist
entries.description: The novel centres an enslaved person's interiority, refusing the plantation record's reduction of them to property, and the craft question is how to render that interior without false documentary confidence.

examples.text: Jones populates a Virginia county with enslaved people whose full inner lives the historical record never kept.
Edugyan follows an enslaved boy from a Barbados plantation into a wider world, his consciousness the book's centre.
set in a later oppression, it centres Black domestic workers but filters them through a white protagonist's redemption.

entries.name: The Soldier's-Eye View
entries.description: War is delivered through one combatant's limited, embodied experience, so the famous campaign is known as mud, fear and rumour rather than as strategy.

examples.text: the single-take conceit locks the viewer to two soldiers' ground-level ignorance of the larger battle.
Cornwell delivers the Danish wars through a warrior who sees only his part of them.
the soldier's view is repeatedly abandoned for reverent tableaux of great commanders.

entries.name: The Spy and the Double Life
entries.description: An agent living a concealed life dramatises a period's politics from inside its secrets, and the constant risk of exposure makes the era's loyalties and dangers concrete.

examples.text: Atwood's servant conceals an interior the authorities cannot read, a double life of survival.
Harris's investigator navigates a regime whose secrets it is lethal to uncover.
the wartime spy romance leans on glamour more than on the period's actual machinery of espionage.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The Doomed Aristocrat
entries.description: A member of a class about to be swept away embodies an order's end through personal decline, so the fall of a world is felt as one refined life's obsolescence.

examples.text: Roth traces a family's decline in step with the Habsburg empire it served.
the cultured world Zhivago belongs to is annihilated around him.
the aristocrat's constrained life is rendered as costume tragedy, the historical stakes subordinated to spectacle.

entries.name: The Self-Made Outsider
entries.description: A character rises through a rigid order by talent or ruthlessness, and their ascent exposes both the order's closed hierarchy and the cost of breaching it.

examples.text: Spufford's stranger climbs and gambles through a small colonial New York that cannot place him.
Kubrick's adventurer talks and marries his way into a gentry that will finally expel him.
the self-made rise is pure anachronistic uplift, the period a backdrop for a modern success fable.

entries.name: The Convert Under Pressure
entries.description: A character changes faith or allegiance under historical duress, and the conversion, sincere, coerced or strategic, dramatises how power reshapes belief.

examples.text: Endō makes apostasy under torture the novel's agonised centre, faith and survival at war.
Undset renders medieval faith as the medium in which penance and belief are lived, not chosen lightly.
the crusader's shifting belief is modern religious scepticism in twelfth-century dress.

entries.name: The Divided Family
entries.description: A family split by a historical schism, war, revolution or partition, lets one household carry a whole society's fracture, so the great division is felt at the dinner table.

examples.text: Jakes divides a friendship and two families across the American Civil War.
Seth's families carry the tensions of a newly partitioned India through their alliances and quarrels.
the divided-family sweep is grand but inseparable from the film's romanticised, Lost Cause South.

entries.name: The Woman Trading in a Man's World
entries.description: A courtesan, merchant or operator makes her way through an economy that grants women no legitimate power, so her leverage and its precariousness map the period's constraints on female agency.

examples.text: Winsor's heroine rises through Restoration London using the only currencies a woman was permitted.
Golden's narrator navigates a pre-war economy of patronage, though the book's outsider vantage has drawn criticism.
the adaptation plays the survivor's economy for romp, loosening the desperation that drove it.

entries.name: The Exile
entries.description: A character cut off from home by history, banishment, flight or conquest, carries a lost world within them, and the ache of exile measures what a political catastrophe destroyed.

examples.text: García Márquez follows Bolívar into a final exile that is also the death of his continental dream.
Némirovsky's refugees carry a vanishing France into flight.
the exile's pathos is real but subordinated to sweeping romance and landscape.

entries.name: The Long Captivity
entries.description: Prolonged imprisonment or captivity becomes a period condition in itself, and the confined life reveals a society through the machinery that holds a person and the world glimpsed beyond the walls.

examples.text: Charrière's penal-colony years render a whole carceral world, though its factual claims are contested.
Valerie Martin confines the reader to a slaveholding household as its own kind of prison.
the captivity is a springboard for revenge adventure rather than a rendered condition.

entries.name: The Maker in History
entries.description: An artist or craftsman works against the patronage, censorship and constraints of their age, so the making of art becomes a window onto the period's power and belief.

examples.text: Stone stages Michelangelo's work as a struggle with patrons, popes and the material itself.
Chevalier reconstructs a painter's household and the labour behind a single canvas.
dazzling but built on the long-discredited legend of Salieri's murder of Mozart, which it presents as drama.
