entries.name: The Healer and the Pre-Modern Body
entries.description: A midwife, herbalist or physician carries a period's knowledge of the body, and their practice, and its collision with authority, opens the era's understanding of life, death and women's expertise.

examples.text: McKay follows a rural midwife as professionalised medicine moves to displace her craft.
Gordon dramatises a medieval apprentice crossing faiths to reach the era's most advanced medicine.
the healer heroine's modern medical knowledge repeatedly rescues the plot, a time-traveller's advantage over the period.

entries.name: The Heretic Against Orthodoxy
entries.description: A freethinker collides with religious or political orthodoxy, and their persecution dramatises the period's limits on thought and the machinery built to enforce them.

examples.text: the film stages the Inquisition's pursuit of heresy as the enforcement of a whole order of knowledge.
the Reformation-era radical of the collective's novel is hunted across a Europe policing belief.
the clash of science and orthodoxy is flattened into a straightforward tale of enlightened hero versus benighted age.

entries.name: The Collaborator
entries.description: A character cooperates with an occupying or oppressive power, and the trope refuses easy judgement, rendering the calculations, fears and compromises that collaboration actually involved.

examples.text: Schlink makes complicity and its later reckoning the novel's difficult centre.
Verhoeven refuses clean lines between resistance and collaboration in occupied Holland.
the occupation romance softens collaboration into star-crossed feeling.

entries.name: The Resistance Fighter
entries.description: A character joins armed or clandestine resistance to a regime, and the trope dramatises the cost, futility and moral complexity of defiance rather than a clean heroism.

examples.text: small acts of resistance in Nazi Germany carry lethal risk and uncertain effect.
Melville renders the French Resistance as grim, attritional and often doomed labour.
the partisan story leans toward conventional heroics, smoothing the ambiguities the history held.

entries.name: The Arrival
entries.description: An immigrant reaches a new country, and the trope reconstructs a historical migration through the shock, hope and dislocation of the newcomer meeting a world that did not expect them.

examples.work: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay
examples.text: Chabon's refugee arrives into a New York the war is about to change.
Davies threads Chinese-American arrival across a century of exclusion and labour.
the immigrant arrival is romanticised into a land-rush adventure that skims its harsh history.

entries.name: The Old Believer
entries.description: A character clings to a dying faith, order or way of life as history sweeps it away, and their refusal to change measures the cost and the dignity of what is being lost.

examples.text: Okonkwo's fidelity to a threatened Igbo order becomes tragic as colonialism dismantles it.
Roth's servants of the empire keep faith with an order already gone.
the clinging-to-an-order premise is undercut by a twist that makes the historical setting a fabrication.

entries.name: The Bound Child
entries.description: A child sold, indentured or apprenticed enters a period's economy of bound labour, and their lack of consent exposes a system the era took as ordinary.

examples.text: Coates centres a young man born into slavery, bound from birth, reaching for freedom.
Ghosh's indentured and bound characters are fed into the machinery of the opium economy.
the bound-child ordeal is rendered with period detail but resolves into sentimental rescue.

entries.name: The Convert's Betrayal
entries.description: A character's change of side or faith forces a betrayal of those left behind, so the personal cost of a historical realignment falls on intimate relationships.

examples.text: Scorsese makes the apostate's betrayal of his fellow Christians the film's central wound.
McBride's narrator survives by shifting allegiances around John Brown, each turn a small betrayal.
the crossing-of-loyalties premise is buried under conventional war action.

entries.name: The Clash at Contact
entries.description: Two civilizations meet for the first time, and the encounter dramatises incommensurable worldviews colliding, with the craft danger of narrating it entirely from one side's frame.

examples.text: the meeting of Jesuits, Guaraní and empire stages a genuine collision of orders, though it centres the Europeans.
Moore renders seventeenth-century contact between a French priest and the Huron as mutual, unbridgeable incomprehension.
visceral and immersive, but its Maya history is contested and shaped toward spectacle.

entries.name: The Archive Quest
entries.description: Characters search for a lost document, manuscript or truth, and the hunt through records dramatises how the past is recovered and how easily it is lost.

examples.text: Zafón sends a boy after a vanished author through a post-war Barcelona of hidden books.
Setterfield's biographer excavates a concealed family history from contradictory testimony.
the archive quest becomes a pure treasure-hunt, history reduced to a series of clues.

entries.name: The Recovered Voice
entries.description: The novel gives narrative to those the archive silenced, making the unrecorded life its centre, and the craft is to render an interior the record denies without false documentary confidence.

examples.text: Morrison reconstructs the interior of the enslaved from testimony and haunting rather than a record that never kept it, the paradigm of the recovered voice.
Butler sends a modern woman into slavery so its silenced experience is made unbearably immediate.
it recovers marginalised voices but leans on melodrama that softens the history.

entries.name: The Proleptic Detail
entries.description: A period-accurate detail is charged with the catastrophe the reader knows is coming, so ordinary life is shadowed by a future the characters cannot see, at the risk of heavy-handed foreshadowing.

examples.text: the Weimar gaiety is shot through with the Nazism the audience knows will end it.
Lutes's teeming Weimar is everywhere marked by the coming catastrophe without saying so.
Death's foreshadowing narration signposts the coming losses too insistently.

entries.name: The Great Man Glimpsed
entries.description: A famous historical figure is seen briefly and obliquely, through ordinary characters, so history's giants appear as others met them rather than as the centre of the frame.

examples.text: Caesar and Augustus are glimpsed through two ordinary soldiers whose lives brush theirs.
the icon-painter moves through a violent age whose great events reach him only at the edges.
the great artists appear as whimsical cameos, charming but weightless.

entries.name: The Battle From the Losing Side
entries.description: A battle or war is narrated from the side that loses, recovering the perspective the victors' record suppresses and asking whose account survives to be told.

examples.work: All Quiet on the Western Front
examples.text: the German trenches deliver the war from the side history records as defeated.
the doomed U-boat crew are rendered as men, not the enemy the Allied record made of them.
sympathetic to the Confederate command in ways that soften the cause it served.

entries.name: The Everyday Under Tyranny
entries.description: Ordinary life is reconstructed under a repressive regime, so the period's terror is felt in queues, denunciations and small fears rather than in spectacle.

examples.text: Fallada renders the ordinary Berliners whose tiny resistance the Reich crushed.
Smith reconstructs the everyday paranoia of Stalinist life, where safety itself is suspect.
it satirises the everyday under Nazism, a tonal choice whose handling of the material is contested.

entries.name: The Last Days of a City
entries.description: A city on the verge of falling concentrates a period's end into one place, its streets and people rendered in the knowledge of the destruction to come.

examples.text: Benioff's besieged Leningrad is a whole world starving in real time.
Bulwer-Lytton's archetypal doomed-city novel builds toward the eruption the reader awaits.
the fall of a city is rendered as spectacle that discards the Homeric frame and its meaning.

entries.name: The Document That Turns the Plot
entries.description: A letter, dispatch or record becomes the hinge of the narrative, and the period's own forms of writing carry the decisive turn, foregrounding how documents make and unmake history.

examples.text: Harris turns a decrypted signal into the pivot of a wartime plot.
James builds a whole intrigue around the coveted letters of a dead poet.
documents are pure plot-fuel, the history a decorative pretext.

entries.name: Faith Tested by History
entries.description: A character's belief is tried by the pressure of historical events, and the test dramatises a period's religious life as lived stakes rather than backdrop.

examples.text: Greene's whisky priest carries a failing faith through a persecuting revolution.
the painter's faith and vocation are tested against an age of cruelty until he can no longer work.
the faith test is flattened into a conventional conversion drama.

entries.name: The Technological Threshold
entries.description: A new invention or technique remakes the world within the novel, and the threshold dramatises how a period was changed by what it learned to make, without lapsing into a museum of gadgets.

examples.text: Follett makes the engineering of a Gothic cathedral the engine of the plot.
the drilling of oil remakes a landscape and a man across the threshold into the modern age.
the invention race is rendered as a flat, dutiful biopic.

entries.name: The Map Redrawn
entries.description: Borders and empires shift within the book, and the redrawing of the map dramatises how abstract political change fell on specific lives, so a partition or a treaty is felt as a wound.

examples.text: Singh renders Partition through a single village torn apart by the new border.
Follett tracks the First World War's redrawing of Europe across linked families.
the map-making is romanticised and the Arab agency it depended on is sidelined.

entries.name: The Famine
entries.description: A community meets starvation, and the famine reconstructs a period's economy and politics through the extremity of hunger, exposing who is let die and why.

examples.text: O'Connor puts the Irish Famine aboard a coffin ship where class decides who survives.
Buck renders famine in China as the force that governs a peasant family's whole existence.
the Famine becomes the backdrop for a revenge thriller.

entries.name: The Ritual as Period Window
entries.description: A ceremony, trial or communal ritual opens a whole period's mentality, since what a society performs together reveals its beliefs, hierarchies and fears more fully than any exposition.

examples.text: Hargrave uses a 1617 witch trial to open the beliefs and terrors of an Arctic Norwegian community.
Harvey structures a medieval village around the ritual of confession, the sacrament shaping the whole book.
folk ritual is deployed as horror spectacle, the history invented for effect.

entries.name: The Trial of Conscience
entries.description: A character faces a moral choice under historical pressure, and the trope makes an era's ethics concrete by forcing a decision the period's own terms make agonising.

examples.text: More's conscience is set against a king's demand in the period's own religious and legal language.
Styron builds the novel around an impossible choice the machinery of Nazism imposed.
the moral reckoning is flattened into courtroom uplift.

entries.name: The Silenced Witness
entries.description: A character sees a history they are given no power to record or tell, and the trope dramatises the archive's silences from inside, through the observer the record erased.

examples.text: James narrates a Jamaican plantation through a witness the historical record would never have preserved.
Morrison gives voice to figures at the very origin of American slavery whom the record left mute.
the witnesses to oppression are softened into a story of uplift.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The Restoration
entries.description: A displaced king, order or rightful claimant returns, and the restoration dramatises a period's ideas of legitimacy and providence, often carrying a myth of natural order restored.

examples.text: Tremain uses the return of Charles II to anatomise a whole culture's swing from austerity to excess.
Scott builds the return of the rightful king into a founding myth of reconciled nation.

examples.work: The Man in the Iron Mask
examples.text: the substitution-and-restoration is played as pure swashbuckling adventure.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The Revolution Devours Its Own
entries.description: A revolution turns on its makers, and the trope dramatises the logic by which upheaval consumes the people who began it, rendering political abstraction as personal doom.

examples.text: Mantel follows the French revolutionaries to the guillotine their own movement raises.
Koestler renders the show trial through an old Bolshevik consumed by the revolution he served.
powerful but compresses the Terror into a duel of two men.

entries.name: The Colonizer's Reckoning
entries.description: A colonising presence is confronted with the human cost of its project, and the trope dramatises empire from the point of its moral crisis, with the danger of centring the colonizer's redemption.

examples.text: Kingsolver turns a missionary family's Congo into an indictment of the whole colonial enterprise.
Grenville forces an English settler in Australia to the violence his claim to the land requires.
the reckoning centres the colonizer's redemption, displacing the people whose loss it depicts.

entries.name: The Unspoken Atrocity
entries.description: An atrocity is never directly spoken of, transmitted instead as silence and inherited damage, and the trope dramatises how catastrophe reaches later generations through what cannot be said.

examples.text: Spiegelman reconstructs his father's Holocaust from interviews, the son extracting a story silence had sealed.
Foer's grandson excavates a shtetl's erased history through a comic and grievous inquiry.
the survivor testimony is fictionalised in ways historians have contested.

entries.name: The Middle Passage
entries.description: A sea voyage, above all the transatlantic slave crossing, becomes a bounded world of confinement and horror, and the trope demands the crossing be rendered as history rather than as backdrop.

examples.text: Johnson sets a freed man aboard a slaver and makes the crossing the book's moral and physical centre.
Hill renders the passage as one link in a life the record tried to erase.
the crossing sequence is powerful but framed by courtroom uplift that eases the horror.

entries.name: The Frontier Encounter
entries.description: Characters meet at the edge of settlement, and the frontier dramatises the collision of peoples, economies and landscapes, increasingly used to correct the myth of the noble conquest.

examples.text: Williams strips the frontier myth to its brutal economic and ecological reality.
Cooper's founding frontier romance stages a contact the genre would spend a century revising.
the frontier encounter is spectacle-driven, the history a canvas for endurance.

entries.category: Rise, Fall & the End of Orders
entries.name: The Court Intrigue
entries.description: Factional maneuvering at a centre of power drives the plot, and the intrigue reconstructs how a period's politics actually worked, through faction, favour and information, at the risk of soap opera.

examples.text: Graves builds the imperial court as a machine of poison, marriage and succession.
the adaptation renders feudal Japanese factionalism as a lethal game of position and patience.
the court intrigue is entertaining but pitched as costume soap.

entries.name: The Meaningful Coincidence
entries.description: Chance meetings and convergences are made to carry historical meaning, and the trope's power and its danger are the same, since coincidence can illuminate a period's connectedness or reduce it to contrivance.

examples.text: Mitchell's echoes across centuries assert a pattern the reader is invited to weigh.
Atkinson's repeated reworkings of a life turn coincidence into a meditation on history's contingency.
the protagonist's collision with every historical moment turns coincidence into the whole conceit.

entries.name: The Endnote of History
entries.description: The book closes by tying its fiction back to the documented record, through an epilogue, author's note or collage of sources, and the trope makes the seam between the made and the found part of the reading.

examples.text: Saunders builds the novel itself from a collage of real and invented sources, the record and the fiction interleaved.
Keneally frames the whole with an apparatus that keeps its factual spine visible.

examples.work: The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas
examples.text: its closing fable-note asserts a lesson the implausible story has not earned.

entries.name: Walter Scott
entries.description: Scottish, 1771–1832; conventionally credited with inventing the historical novel as a form.
entries.meta: Scottish, 1771–1832. Poet turned novelist conventionally credited with inventing the historical novel as a form; published the Waverley novels anonymously at first.
entries.knownFor: The Waverley sequence and the model of an ordinary protagonist caught between contending historical forces.
entries.signature: Antiquarian density married to a middling hero through whom the reader meets the great figures of an age; the past rendered as a society with its own logic.

entries.name: Alessandro Manzoni
entries.description: Italian, 1785–1873. Author of the founding Italian historical novel and a central figure in the making of a modern Italian literary language.
entries.meta: Italian, 1785–1873. Author of the founding Italian historical novel and a central figure in the making of a modern Italian literary language.
entries.knownFor: The Betrothed, set in seventeenth-century plague-era Lombardy under Spanish rule.
entries.signature: Scott's method turned to a moral and providential vision, with a linguistic project of national standardisation behind the definitive revision.

entries.name: Alexandre Dumas
entries.description: French, 1802–1870; the great popular historical novelist of the nineteenth-century serial.
entries.meta: French, 1802–1870. The great popular historical novelist of the nineteenth century, working prolifically in the serial feuilleton, often with collaborators.
entries.knownFor: The Musketeers cycle and The Count of Monte Cristo, the swashbuckler tradition's fountainhead.
entries.signature: Momentum, intrigue and honour over documentary fidelity; history as a playground for pace and set-piece.

entries.name: Victor Hugo
entries.description: French, 1802–1885. Poet, dramatist and novelist whose historical fictions fused Romantic sweep with social argument.
entries.meta: French, 1802–1885. Poet, dramatist and novelist whose historical fictions fused Romantic sweep with social argument.
entries.knownFor: The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, a reconstruction of late-medieval Paris, and Ninety-Three, on the Revolution.
entries.signature: Vast set-pieces, the city or the era as protagonist, and history harnessed to a moral and political vision.

entries.name: James Fenimore Cooper
entries.description: American, 1789–1851. The first major American historical novelist, adapting Scott to the American frontier.
entries.meta: American, 1789–1851. The first major American historical novelist, adapting Scott to the American frontier.
entries.knownFor: The Leatherstocking Tales, above all The Last of the Mohicans.
entries.signature: Frontier romance and landscape, staging the contact of peoples that later American historical fiction would spend a century revising.

entries.name: Gustave Flaubert
entries.description: French, 1821–1880. Master of realist prose who turned to the remote past in one great reconstruction.
entries.meta: French, 1821–1880. Master of realist prose who turned to the remote past in one great reconstruction.
entries.knownFor: Salammbô, a dense reconstruction of third-century-BC Carthage during the Mercenary War.
entries.signature: Archaeological immersion and controlled prose, pursuing a total reconstruction of an alien and exotic world.

entries.name: Leo Tolstoy
entries.description: Russian, 1828–1910; author of the form's summit and its great boundary case from living memory.
entries.meta: Russian, 1828–1910. Author of the nineteenth century's summit of the form and its great boundary case, drawn from family and living memory rather than an archive.
entries.knownFor: War and Peace, set during the Napoleonic invasion of roughly half a century before its writing.
entries.signature: Vast social canvas with the world-historical figures at the margins; the ordinary experience of history as it happens to people.

entries.name: Alexander Pushkin
entries.description: Russian, 1799–1837. Foundational figure of Russian literature who wrote an early Russian historical novel.
entries.meta: Russian, 1799–1837. Foundational figure of Russian literature who wrote an early Russian historical novel.
entries.knownFor: The Captain's Daughter, set during the Pugachev rebellion of the 1770s.
entries.signature: Economy and clarity, a Scott-influenced reconstruction rendered in spare, ironic prose.

entries.name: Nikolai Gogol
entries.description: Russian, of Ukrainian origin, 1809–1852. Wrote a foundational Cossack historical romance alongside his satirical work.
entries.meta: Russian, of Ukrainian origin, 1809–1852. Wrote a foundational Cossack historical romance alongside his satirical work.
entries.knownFor: Taras Bulba, a Romantic epic of the Zaporozhian Cossacks.
entries.signature: Heightened Romantic nationalism and folkloric colour, the past rendered as heroic myth.

entries.name: Prosper Mérimée
entries.description: French, 1803–1870. Novelist and archaeologist who wrote a notable French historical novel of the Wars of Religion.
entries.meta: French, 1803–1870. Novelist and archaeologist who wrote a notable French historical novel of the Wars of Religion.
entries.knownFor: A Chronicle of the Reign of Charles IX, on the Saint Bartholomew's Day massacre.
entries.signature: Dry, ironic economy and a scholar's eye, resisting Romantic excess.

works.title: A Chronicle of the Reign of Charles IX

entries.name: Alfred de Vigny
entries.description: French, 1797–1863. Romantic poet who produced one of the earliest French historical novels after Scott.
entries.meta: French, 1797–1863. Romantic poet who produced one of the earliest French historical novels after Scott.
entries.knownFor: Cinq-Mars, on a conspiracy against Richelieu under Louis XIII.
entries.signature: Romantic tragedy and a pessimistic view of power, history as the ruin of noble figures.

entries.name: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
entries.description: English, 1803–1873. Enormously popular Victorian novelist and dramatist, a central populariser of the historical novel.
entries.meta: English, 1803–1873. Enormously popular Victorian novelist and dramatist, a central populariser of the historical novel.
entries.knownFor: The Last Days of Pompeii, the archetypal doomed-city reconstruction.
entries.signature: Melodrama and spectacle over a diligent antiquarian frame, the disaster or the era as engine.

works.title: Harold, the Last of the Saxon Kings

entries.name: William Makepeace Thackeray
